speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister. Has the government been advised of the date of arrival of the commonwealth mission which is coming to Canada to prepare for Britain's entry into the common market, and is the government in a position to state what is Canada's attitude?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: MISSION TO DISCUSS ENTRY BY U.K.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman has asked me a question identical to that of which the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot has given notice.
The government is aware that the United Kingdom government is considering how best to arrange for effective consultation with other commonwealth governments on the subject of the European common market and the United Kingdom joining that market. I might say that I have made it clear to the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, and he has agreed, that there should be consultation before any move in that direction is taken by the government of the United Kingdom.
There has been continuing consultation at the level of officials. The most recent discussion in this series took place in London two weeks ago during the meeting of senior economic advisers of the commonwealth countries. As to consultation on a ministerial level between the United Kingdom and Canada, to which the hon. gentleman made reference, nothing definite has yet been arranged.
I might say in that connection that while consultation on a bilateral basis would be helpful in order to take account of the special
interests of individual countries, I believe that instead of limiting consultation to separate meetings among interested commonwealth countries, the best means would be collective consultation among all interested commonwealth countries. I envisage bilateral consultation, official and ministerial, but because of the potential consequences of United Kingdom membership in the common market, I believe that the fullest consideration should be given to collective ministerial discussion and also, if necessary, to a meeting of the prime ministers.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO INCREASE IN DELIVERY QUOTAS
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Agriculture. Is the minister prepared to tell the house what progress is being made by the Canadian wheat board in providing increased quotas for western grain?

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO INCREASE IN DELIVERY QUOTAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I reported to the house several days ago that we have made fairly good progress. We had a splendid series of days between May 8 and May 11. I have the figures for June 8. The house will recall that the last time I reported the big effort was to get all the points from 2 bushels into 3 bushels. I am now able to report that in Manitoba, where on May 29, a little over a week ago, we had 121 points on 3 bushels, now there are none. In Saskatchewan a little over a week ago, on May 29, we had 190 points on 3 bushels and now there are 4, so that all through the west at the present time there are only 4 points on 3 bushels. The number of points on 4 bushels is now 762, the number on 5 bushels is 589, and the number on 6 bushels is 639.
I can say at this time that the situation in relation to Alberta is much better than it was last year, but in Manitoba and Saskatchewan it is still not as good as it was last year. However, tremendous efforts are being made by the grain handling companies on the prairies, the railways and the terminals, and they have now produced a situation where some 1,600 cars a day-and that is not far off 3 million bushels a day-are moving into the terminals. The eastern farmers have built up a demand for oats, so we gave a supplementary quota of 5 bushels per acre in order to try to get this supply into the elevators to make sure eastern farmers were supplied. This of course means that less wheat will be moved, to the extent of oats delivered. I should like to point out in conclusion that this year the producer marketings of grain is much higher than it has been for a long time at this time of year.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO INCREASE IN DELIVERY QUOTAS
speechtext:
May I ask
a supplementary question. I wonder whether the minister could tell the house this, since the end of the crop year is just some seven or eight weeks away. Does he still confidently expect that quotas and marketing opportunities will reach 7 bushels an acre?

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO INCREASE IN DELIVERY QUOTAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I gave an answer to this question three or four days ago, to the effect that the advisory committee of the Canadian wheat board had

unanimously recommended that the first job of the Canadian wheat board was to sell grain. That means that if we get a market for oats in eastern Canada or for any other type of cash crop, this would get preference and be moved out. However, I still think it is physically possible in most cases to reach the 7 bushels. If there is some place that does not meet it, it is because we have given higher priority to the total number of bushels of all grain that the western farmer is allowed to sell.
Mr. W. M. Benidickson (Kenora-Rainy
River): Mr. Speaker, may I ask a supplementary question inasmuch as it similarly involves cash flowing into the hands of the western farmers at this time. DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE 273. Bankruptcy Act administration, $118,770.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE AGAINST REDUCTION OR LOSS OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
When these estimates were last before the committee I had my little say on this item, but during recent days I had a gentleman visit me from Montreal, a Mr. A. G. Heakes. I am raising a question of which I am sure the minister has some knowledge. I have talked to Mr. Heakes and I have read a number of documents and

letters, and he had hundreds of them. I simply lacked the time to go through the documents properly and read them and all the material that he had with him so that I could understand all aspects of this case. However, this gentleman does suffer from a sense of injustice and, from the material I had the opportunity to read and partly digest, I am of the opinion that Mr. Heakes has grounds for complaint. For that reason I promised him that I would raise this matter on the minister's estimates. I am going to bring the case briefly to the attention of the committee, because it is lengthy and most complicated.
In August, 1954, the Imperial Oil Company breached a contract with Mr. Heakes, and it was this breach of contract which forced Mr. Heakes into bankruptcy. He made a proposal to his creditors, as provided in the act. On February 7, 1955 Mr. Heakes submitted a proposal to his creditors to pay 100 cents on the dollar in four payments of 5 per cent and 20 per cent every four months over a 12-month period. A creditors' meeting was called for March 8, 1955. According to Mr. Heakes this meeting was never held. Then on May 31, 1955, Mr. Heakes made an amended proposal to the creditors offering full and final payment from the proceeds of actions to be taken against Imperial Oil, the Royal Bank and so on. It was a rather complicated arrangement, and I am not going to go into the details.
On November 22, 1955 this proposal was ratified by Chief Justice W. B. Scott in the superior court with the condition, endorsed in his own handwriting, that the actions must be started and served within 20 days from the date of ratification. On December 12, 1955 writs and declarations were served. In January, 1956, owing to worry over this business, Mr. Heakes apparently suffered a complete physical and nervous collapse and was hospitalized for several months.
In November, 1957 the corporation of professional engineers of Quebec began an investigation of the dispute of Mr. Heakes with the engineer of the Imperial Oil Company, Quebec marketing division. On January 25, 1958, approximately, Mr. Heakes says that a formal trial of this action was held before the full council of the corporation of professional engineers, following a report of the investigation by the committee on professional conduct of the corporation of professional engineers of Quebec whose chairman was Mr. Yvon Tasse, now Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works. Then Mr. Heakes' premises were broken into and his evidence was stolen.
On January 1, 1958 he laid charges against the thief and there were postponements
Supply-J ustice
awaiting the verdict of the corporation of engineers. On February 4, 1958 there was another development with respect to this offence. He wired the trustee to this effect: Receipt for documents urgently required for police.
On March 28, 1958 a verdict was issued by the corporation of professional engineers completely upholding Mr. Heakes in his complaint against the Imperial Oil Company. Mr. Heakes has a copy of this verdict.
On April 9, 1958 hearing of the charge against thief was called on the day before the date set by the judge and on court subpoenas. The charge was dismissed because no one was there. On June 9, 1958 the trustee obtained an ex parte cancellation of the proposal alleging he did not know where to find Mr. Heakes and that Mr. Heakes had failed to make payments required by the proposal. On September 4, 1959 Mr. Heakes met Mr. Guy Favreau, assistant deputy minister of justice, through the present Minister of Trade and Commerce, and he spent the entire day with Mr. Favreau checking over this matter. On March 14, 1960 this gentleman was employed for a short time by the royal commission on transportation and submitted a report.
I have looked at a great deal of detail with respect to the sequence of events in this case which would not assist the committee in any way if I were to read it. After reading the documents I must say I am of the opinion that this gentleman has grounds for complaint. From what I have read it appears to me that the trustee has not properly performed his duties under the Bankruptcy Act, and that the registrar in question has been somewhat delinquent.
Is the trustee in bankruptcy an employee of the government? Is he directly responsible to the government for his actions when acting as trustee? Will the minister consider a further investigation of this case? Can he give us from his knowledge of the case, which I understand is quite extensive-and this applies to other members of the cabinet-some explanation why this gentleman, who is in very serious financial circumstances and, from what I have read of the case, unfairly so, has been unable to obtain justice and get the matter satisfactorily settled?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE AGAINST REDUCTION OR LOSS OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise also to speak to the case which the hon. member for Kootenay West has already mentioned. I have no doubt that the gentleman in question has importuned many members of this house in the past. From the resume of his file which I have seen I would say that he has had considerable consideration given to him both by the Minister of Justice

Supply-Justice
and by other members of the cabinet. It is this very fact, Mr. Chairman, that leads me to believe that in the government's checking into this file on the matter they have come across some evidence indicating that there is some truth to support the allegations made by Mr. Heakes.
Like the hon. member for Kootenay West, I undertook to at least raise this matter in the house. It would appear, Mr. Chairman, that one of the greatest responsibilities of any department, and particularly of the Department of Justice, is to uphold that greatest of legal principles that not only must justice be done but it must appear to be done. If for seven or eight years a man has been pursuing his remedy in and out of the courts and in this parliament, the supreme court of this country, with diligence and with documentary evidence, then it would appear that he is motivated by a real sense of having suffered an injustice.
I am not particularly familiar with the provisions of the Bankruptcy Act, but I have noted that under the subsections of section 3 the superintendent of bankruptcy, who is charged under that section with supervision of the administration of the assets to which the act applies, is empowered to make a complete investigation of any particular matter. Neither the material which Mr. Heakes has provided me nor that to which I have had recourse indicates that in fact such an investigation has ever taken place.
I would ask the minister, who I am sure is much more familiar with the file than I, whether consideration has yet been given or will be given in the department to having a full scale investigation made by the superintendent of bankruptcy with respect to the actions of the trustee acting on behalf of the creditors in this matter. So far as I am able to ascertain, the legal effect of this is that Mr. Heakes is insolvent but he is not bankrupt under the act and is in no position to be discharged. This means, then, that he is in a period of hiatus, is incapable of starting his own business again, and will always remain a credit risk. It means that a man of his capabilities will always remain incapable of getting a job or of keeping one or of starting his own business.
The government has already shown a great deal of consideration with regard to this matter. Both the ministry, representatives of the Prime Minister's office and other persons have indicated their extreme sympathy. It would appear, therefore, that in the special circumstances this matter might be resolved by going further than sympathy and having an actual judicial investigation, which is permitted under the act. The Bankruptcy

Act often works to the disadvantage of honest people in the community. This may be one of those cases, and I have another I should like to put before the minister for consideration at such time as the Bankruptcy Act may be amended.
As all hon. members know, the Bankruptcy Act was instituted in order that an individual might be assisted who, usually without fault, goes into such debt that he is incapable of discharging his obligations now or at any time in the future because his liabilities so greatly outweigh his assets. The act was instituted to aid the honest man who has done his best and is unable now and in the future to meet his obligations. However, because of the provisions of the act there are those who are able to take advantage of them to the prejudice of the public and beyond the purpose intended by the legislation.
May I for one minute refer to a case which came to my attention in practice before I was a member of the house. A widow who owned a very small cottage enlisted the aid of a man who held himself out to be a painting contractor. He had a truck and all the necessary equipment. She hired him to strip the paint from her dwelling house. He did this by means of a blow torch, and because of his negligence he burned down the house.
She then brought an action against him in the supreme court of Ontario and was successful in obtaining a judgment. The painter and his wife jointly owned their home, and they put a mortgage on it in order to pay part of their solicitor's fees and also in order to lodge an appeal. The appeal was a frivolous one, but many months went by before the appeal was heard. The judgment of the trial court was confirmed and the day following the defendant, against whom judgment had been given in the amount of $10,000 and costs, went into bankruptcy. The only debt he owed over and above his normal debts, such as mortgages on his home, one of which had been placed there for the purpose of proceeding with this litigation, and small telephone accounts and so on that everyone has at any given time, was the judgment in question.
There is no way in which such a person can be denied his rights under the Bankruptcy Act. In fact the only thing that can be done is to apply to the court when the applicant comes before it for discharge and, according to the case law, only in the rarest instance will discharge be delayed for more than a month or so.
These circumstances indicate that an individual who has been grossly wronged may be left without any recourse at all in law

while the person who has been the wrongdoer is able to escape and, after a hiatus of a few months, become a discharged bankrupt and enter again into exactly the same sort of business and thus prey upon the public again without in fact having lost anything. In effect this means that the law, by permitting an individual in such circumstances to go into bankruptcy, is in fact discriminating against the person who has been wronged.
So far as I am aware, Mr. Chairman, there is no provision in the Bankruptcy Act which sets out which individuals may have recourse to it. It is appreciated that it cannot be so rigidly drawn as to say what cases may come under it and what may not. However, I submit for the consideration of the minister and his department that where the Bankruptcy Act is resorted to for the purpose really of defrauding members of the public, there should be provision that an individual in the circumstances of this widow who was wronged may apply to the court in the first instance, so that the provisions of the Bankruptcy Act will not apply and so that a person who is a judgment debtor will be required to work for some months or some years in an attempt to satisfy the judgment, or will be required to show just cause to the court why he will never be able to satisfy the judgment. Further, there should be provision that an individual shall not be discharged in order to enter into the same business so long as such a judgment remains unsatisfied.
These matters are perhaps not of the type with which I should take up the time of the committee, but they are instances where the Bankruptcy Act, intended for a particular purpose, has been used in the one case against the interests of a wronged individual and in the other case against the interests of a bankrupt person.
In support of what the hon. member for Kootenay West has said, I urge upon the minister that in the case of Mr. Heakes consideration be given to a full scale investigation by the superintendent. As to the second case I mentioned, I urge that consideration be given by the department along the lines I suggested, particularly with respect to an application being made to a court by a judgment debtor, to prevent the operation of the Bankruptcy Act for a judgment creditor.

Mr. Chairman, I am very glad this matter has been raised. I do not intend to speak on the Heakes case, as I have no information about it, but I sincerely hope that a very careful study will be made. I hope action will be taken soon to correct the vicious practice which has developed with regard to proceedings under the Bankruptcy Act. I can say very definitely that a most
Supply-Justice
vicious practice has developed in British Columbia, particularly in the city of Vancouver, a practice that involves certain companies engaged in the construction industry.
There are in Vancouver a few completely irresponsible individuals whom I might almost call legal crooks. What they do is form a company and put in bids on construction work, particularly plumbing and heating. They undercut the bids of honest and responsible contractors, and they do so knowing full well that they cannot do the job for the price. The result is that they go into bankruptcy. Evidence is readily available in Vancouver that at the same time they go into bankruptcy they organize a new company; exactly the same individuals organize a new company and repeat the process all over again. When I was in Vancouver recently I was told that by devious means the new company on occasion gets hold of the very same material and stock of the company which went into bankruptcy, and then they repeat the process over and over again. I have been told about one company which has done this four times.
I think this is an abuse of legitimate business. I was told by those in the construction industry in British Columbia who are operating in an honest, decent legitimate manner that their very existence is being threatened by these people who are allowed to go into bankruptcy and then, within as short a space of time as a week, and in one case of which I have knowledge the very next day, start over again and follow the same procedure.
If there does not now exist legislation or regulations which can be strictly enforced to halt this practice and protect the legitimate operators in the contracting business, the department should investigate the matter and introduce the required policies and measures. When it is found that individuals are repeatedly following this practice there should be some provision preventing them from going back into business until they have demonstrated their honesty and integrity.
Because cases of this nature have been brought to my attention with increasing frequency during the past year, and particularly in recent weeks, I feel this is a developing threat that will endanger legitimate business. I urge the minister to comment on this subject and advise the committee whether it is possible for the department to take remedial action.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE AGAINST REDUCTION OR LOSS OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Chairman. Perhaps I could start with the last inquiry first and then lead back to the case of Mr. Heakes.
With respect to the investigation of irregularities under the Bankruptcy Act, let me say there have been four prosecutions. Four individual trustees have been prosecuted, charges have been laid against a fifth and an investigation is under way in respect to a sixth which will lead either to charges or cancellation of licence. It has not been finally determined what is the appropriate course to be followed.
With respect to the progress report, I should point out to the committee that although I have referred to charges or investigations with respect to only six individuals, in the case particularly of two of them they were trustees engaged in a very large volume of business. They had hundreds if not thousands of files under their control which they were administering, somewhere in the neighbourhood of 400 or more estates each and every one of those files had to be examined. In those two cases particularly a considerable number of charges were laid. It has been necessary for us to retain the services of accountants as well as lawyers to check the files and make the examination necessary to support the charges, and also to advise or assist in an interim capacity to carry on the administration of the estates which, of course, could not be left dormant or arrested simply because the original trustee was under investigation.
With respect to the problems raised by the hon. member for Niagara Falls and the hon. member for Vancouver East, I am aware of the sort of difficulty they have referred to. The problem is not so difficult of solution in the case of an individual, but it is difficult in the case of a corporation. That is the problem of effectively preventing persons who may have formed a corporation which goes bankrupt from forming another corporation and continuing with the same type of business. While

the problem is difficult because of the nature of corporate law I am not saying it is impossible of solution.
The general study of the Bankruptcy Act has been going forward concurrently with the investigation of individual trustees and the two together will, we hope, put us in a position where we can make an intelligent and valuable revision of the Bankruptcy Act in the not too distant future. The points that have been mentioned here will be specifically borne in mind in the course of that revision.
Turning now to the Heakes case, I should say at once we have here a most difficult case in connection with an individual for whom I have a great deal of sympathy. The case has been exhaustively investigated by myself and at least one of my colleagues. It has also been exhaustively studied by senior officials in the government service. I have had a lengthy interview with Mr. Heakes. I referred him to the then assistant deputy minister of justice, who had several lengthy interviews with him. In the course of these interviews the position was fully explained to Mr. Heakes with every regard for the difficult position in which he found himself. Furthermore, I know that at least one of my colleagues has given assistance of a personal nature to Mr. Heakes during the period when he has found himself in difficulty, so it may be said that Mr. Heakes has not found an unsympathetic attitude on the part of the government and its officials.
In summary, however-and Mr. Heakes has been advised of this-the remedy for his difficulty lies in his own hands. We have indicated that we are prepared to do everything we can by way of offering advice to him to assist in this matter, but that unless and until he seeks to apply the remedies that are open to him nothing in fact can be done in order to improve his position.
Our investigation has established that at the time the proposal was made there was some confusion as to whether it was the original or amended proposal which was approved by the court. Our investigation also established that there was some error on the part of the trustee who applied later on to have the proposal annulled. But the action of the trustee, so far as I can determine- and at this point I am satisfied of this on the report of my advisors-was in error and not of the nature of fraud or bad intent.
This having been ascertained, it was suggested to Mr. Heakes that he should apply to the bankruptcy court either for an order reinstating the proposal or, in effect, for an order for a new proposal to be set up. Either course would have the result that his affairs could be dealt with in bankruptcy court and he would then be in a position to prosecute certain other actions which he feels he has and

which, as I understand it, form the only possible assets that he might realize.
Mr. Heakes has consistently taken the position that it is not his responsibility to take this action on his own behalf, that it is somehow or other the responsibility of the Department of Justice and the government to fight his case from now on. He appears to feel that because there was involved a trustee in bankruptcy who may have been guilty of some error, as I have said, it shifts the responsibility to the Department of Justice.
Here is where I should reply to the question asked me by the hon. member for Kootenay West. Trusties in bankruptcy are not officials of the government. They are appointed under the Bankruptcy Act. They are not paid by the government. They are not paid servants. Their remuneration is derived from fees out of the estates they administer. Moreover, they are not subject to detailed control in respect of their operations or to direction by the minister or the superintendent of bankruptcy. They are, however, subject to ultimate supervision as to the propriety of their conduct, but in effect the only control we can exercise is to remove them, cancel their licences or refuse to renew their licences if they are guilty of improper conduct.
As I say, nothing has been brought to my attention, from the full investigation in this case that we have made, to suggest that there was any improper conduct on the part of this particular trustee. But even if there had been improper conduct the only thing that I could and should then do would be to remove that trustee. This would not in any way alter the situation in which Mr. Heakes finds himself and in which, as I say, there are several courses open by means of which to pursue his case and bring about an adjustment of it. However, so far he has steadfastly declined to do so, taking the position that it is the responsibility of this department to conduct his case. We, of course, have no such authority or jurisdiction. I am not aware of any way in which, even with the best of intentions, I as Minister of Justice can go into court on behalf of an individual, particularly when the individual has it within his own power to do that for himself.
I have said that Mr. Heakes has had a most sympathetic hearing by members of the government themselves and by officials in the government service. I also know for a fact that he has been offered help from other quarters. When it became established that it was necessary for him to pursue his remedies in the courts we were concerned, because sometimes that is slightly cold advice to offer to a person who goes through this sort of misfortune which leaves him without the means of effectively pursuing his remedies.
Supply-Justice
But I know for a fact that Mr. Heakes has been offered assistance by friends in this regard; that is to say, they have said they would be prepared to assist him with respect to litigation if he desired to retain competent counsel and pursue that litigation. However, Mr. Heakes has apparently felt that assistance should take other forms, and that any litigation is the responsibility of the government.
I can only repeat my words expressing the sympathy I have for Mr. Heakes, and also repeat to the committee my assurance and my firm belief that everything has been done that possibly could be done for Mr. Heakes in the way of advice, consideration and study of his case, and that future action lies in his own hands.
I should also say that when these matters or facts were established as the result of our investigation, we wrote to the trustee concerned and suggested that in the event of Mr. Heakes retaining another lawyer, the trustee should accord him all possible cooperation in obtaining an extension of time in which to appeal from judgment of the bankruptcy court. The trustee replied on December 22, 1959 to the effect that he would defer his own application for discharge as trustee for as long as would be necessary to give Mr. Heakes appropriate time in which to retain counsel. There was no obligation on the trustee to do this, but he said that under the circumstances, as there had been an error here, he would maintain the status quo so as to facilitate the making of any application that Mr. Heakes might wish to make. That was in December, 1959, and no application has yet been made.

My point is this. The whole question of the administration of the act has been raised. The situation with regard to the appointment and qualifications of trustees naturally gives anyone in my position some concern because they are in a trust capacity. I am glad to be able to assure my hon. friend from Greenwood that the number of apparently dishonest trustees, or the number of trustees who are guilty of irregularities, is far outweighed by the number of honest and reliable trustees in connection with whose administration no question ever arises. It is, however, the unfortunate fact that in the case of two of the six trustees, although they are but a very small percentage of the total number of trustees, the size of their business was such that the number of estates

under their control represented a substantial percentage of the total bankruptcy estates in that area.
I have worked out with the superintendent and other officials of my department, as a result of discussions, what I believe is an improved method of investigating the qualifications of applicants for licence as trustees, and that system is now functioning quite smoothly. I am not going to say that no mistake will ever be made, but I think we have done what can reasonably be done to eliminate the possibility of appointing as trustee a man whose character would indicate that he should not be appointed to a position of trust.
As to his technical qualifications it is sometimes more difficult to make a judgment, and there may be room for error there. A perfectly honest man may just not be competent to do the job, and of course difficulties could arise there. However, in so far as it is possible to do so under the scheme of the present Bankruptcy Act, with respect to appointments and renewals of appointments I think we have a system which is an improvement over the one previously in effect. I think we have a fairly good system of ascertaining that we shall not be appointing anyone unless he is a proper person to appoint in the capacity of trustee.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE AGAINST REDUCTION OR LOSS OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is the first item in the penitentiaries branch and I undertook to the committee to make a short statement by way of a progress report in introducing this item. In discussing the situation with respect to penitentiaries and correctional reform I should perhaps start by saying that it has been the government's intention during the last few years to achieve two major steps forward in the transformation of Canada's penal system into an up-to-date and effective correctional program.
The first of these has been to arouse in the people of Canada themselves an interest in this long neglected branch of government, and to make Canadians aware of their responsibilities in this aspect of the continuing fight against crime. I think all hon. members of this house will have become aware that national interest in and support for the program of reform in our penitentiary system is at an all-time high, and I take this opportunity of thanking all those who have lent their support in fostering this enthusiasm.
The second objective has been a great deal more concrete and equally important. This has been the implementation of the plans and reforms which have been designed during the past few years. Our reforms are not complete, but in reporting to this committee which is asked to vote the money I am happy to be able to outline a series of positive achievements in terms of new penitentiaries, new methods, programs and activities; new ideas actually carried into effect. In other words, plans and preparations are now being matched by performance.
To be more specific, during the last year it has been our objective to develop for the inmates of all our federal institutions a program of training directed positively toward the goal of reforming and rehabilitating as many as possible of the inmates who are in our charge. The corollary of this is of course
Supply-J ustice
to make them fit upon discharge to take their places in our free society as law abiding citizens.
A second objective has been to develop a highly trained and competent staff to man our institutions and administer the positive programs of inmate training which have been authorized. Our third objective has been to provide suitable physical institutions where those sensible and progressive programs of training can be carried on effectively by that trained staff.
I think the most effective method of illustrating the progress made during the last year or two in achieving these objectives is by the simple process of comparison between the present and the past. I believe that the two pictures are more persuasive than anything else I could say in favour of continuing support for a dynamic program of penal reform.
Some 15 months ago 6,200 inmates were confined in federal penitentiaries. All but 400 of these were incarcerated in maximum security institutions across the country. Some of these maximum security institutions can only be described as out-dated fortresses maintained by an armed garrison, with innumerable locks and iron bars, with necessarily limited opportunities for effective training programs, which were carried out in an atmosphere of repression.
In these institutions the inmates were locked in their cells for the greater part of the 24 hours each day, only being allowed to exercise for brief periods, with virtually no provision for rehabilitative training as members of society, and where far too much of the time was spent in unrewarding and unproductive procedures.
The remaining 400, the fortunate few, were housed in the newly opened medium security institution at Joyceville, Ontario, and in the new minimum security institutions at William Head in British Columbia and Valley-field in Quebec, which we had designed and opened even though we were still much occupied with this planning stage. A few months later Springhill institution in Nova Scotia was opened, which gave some further relief to this depressing picture. This was the situation as we had inherited it and as we had modified it during the first two and one half years while we were primarily engaged in studying and developing our plans.
Today, two of these eight maximum security institutions have been transformed to medium security. At Collins Bay penitentiary in Ontario and at the federal training centre in Quebec, the armed and unyielding accoutrements of maximum security have given way to newer and more effective methods of reform.

Supply-Justice
In the space of one year the number of inmates kept under medium security conditions has increased from 200 to almost 1,600, or an increase of 800 per cent, and the 200 kept in minimum security has increased by almost 100 per cent, thanks to the coming into operation of the new Springhill institution. At the present, therefore, the federal penitentiary system consists of six maximum security, four medium security and four minimum security institutions.
During the coming months it is intended to place the emphasis upon the development of minimum security institutions. The committee will have gathered from my previous remarks that the pressure for medium security institutions has in some measure been relieved, and our greatest need is for institutions in which the benefits of minimum security conditions can be brought to bear upon those inmates who have responded to our new rehabilitation methods. The necessary provision has now been made so that, across the country, we shall be opening five correctional work camps, each designed to provide accommodation and training for 80 inmates. These camps will be located at Agassiz, B.C.; Petawawa and Bracebridge, Ontario; Gatineau Park, Quebec, and at another site in Quebec which has not yet been finally selected but with respect to which discussions are now under way.
I would like to assure the house that none of the men held in these institutions will be engaged upon work which would deprive other Canadians of employment. None of the projects which they undertake would be commenced within ten years if they had to be paid for out of tax moneys at the current rates of civilian pay.
In addition to these work camps, five minimum security farm camps will be established, one at each of the five institutions which operate farms. The institutions involved are Dorchester penitentiary in New Brunswick, St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary in Quebec, Collin's Bay penitentiary in Ontario, Manitoba penitentiary and Saskatchewan penitentiary at Prince Albert.
When these steps become fully effective and when, as we expect, we have transformed one other maximum security institution into a medium security penitentiary, our inmate population will, by the end of 1961, be allocated as follows: 3,500 in maximum security, 2,000 in medium security and 1,100 in minimum security conditions.
I would like to add at this time a word about drug addiction. It is the intention of the government, as will have been seen from the debates on the narcotics bill, to build in the lower mainland of British Columbia a drug addiction treatment centre in which will

be confined those persons who are drug addicts and who have been sentenced to penitentiaries for criminal offences. This institution should be ready for occupancy within about two years, and in it we shall try to provide treatment and training for addicts which will assist them to overcome the drug habit. We will also have achieved what to me is an essential reform, in the segregation of the drug addict from the remainder of our inmate population.
Let me now turn to the equally important problem of supplying our penitentiaries with a skilled and dedicated staff. When the correctional planning committee investigated the staff situation it was found that an unfortunate degree of stagnation existed. Moreover, although there had been a staff college in existence since 1948, the available facilities did not permit more than 21 officers to be on a course at one time. This has led to the unfortunate state of affairs that up to this time less than half of our penitentiary officers have received formal training at the hands of the college.
This has now been changed. With respect to staff generally, a system has been worked out under which a full career will be available in the correctional system as a whole. After recruiting and training, emphasis will be upon opportunities for transfers and promotions, not only within institutions but to a much greater extent than before between institutions and regions and between the field and headquarters, so that not only will our present staff be encouraged but a young man joining the service may also have the prospect before him of rising to the very summit.
Just since last September, for instance, eight of Canada's penitentiaries have received new wardens by either transfer or new appointment between institutions; a number of new appointments from within the service will be made when the new camps are opened; all of which opens further opportunities for transfer and promotion to junior officers now in the service. At the present time 14 officers are changing their institutions to take over the position of assistant warden at other institutions. During the coming summer 12 officers will leave their present institutions to become superintendents of administration and supply officers at the new correctional work camps and farm camps.
The revised Penitentiary Act to which the house gave first reading yesterday will, when adopted, put the seal of approval on the new staff and regional organization system.
In order to benefit further from the opportunities thus opened, the staff college at Kingston is to be very considerably enlarged so as to accommodate twice as many trainees as at present. A regional staff college for

French speaking officers from Quebec is in course of being established on the St. Vincent de Paul reserve. A director of staff training has been appointed at headquarters in Ottawa. His task will be to co-ordinate staff training at all levels of the service.
In accord with our advanced theories of penal reform, special emphasis has been placed upon building up our professional and semi-professional counselling staff. At the moment we have 75 positions for supervisors of classification, psychologists, classification officers and assistant classification officers.
One item which might seem small but whose effect on morale may be considerable is that the formidable military type uniforms of the penitentiary staff are to be replaced by a uniform cut in a civilian pattern made of a smart blue material. It is expected that by the end of 1962 this style of uniform will be available to all officers who serve in medium security institutions. All the uniforms will be made in the institutions themselves.
Finally, I should also mention some of the actual programs which are being put into effect in Canadian penitentiaries. Within the last four months a program of evening activity for inmates has been established in every one of our institutions except St. Vincent de Paul. Unfortunately, in that institution conditions caused by overcrowding render such programs impossible. We are moving as rapidly as possible to meet that situation and put St. Vincent on the same basis as all our other institutions.
Formerly an inmate's day ended at 4.30 in the afternoon when he was locked in his cell, where he remained until seven o'clock next morning. Now, however, his day is extended to 9.30 or ten o'clock in the evening, and in the intervening hours he is encouraged to take part in group activities, sports and study opportunities. In many of our institutions citizens from local communities come into the penitentiary and bring with them their knowledge of special arts and skills.
A prison system which has not solved the problem of prison labour cannot be said to be operating institutions of correction and reform. There is little chance of effecting the rehabilitation in society of an inmate who upon his release is unwilling, unable or unfit to accept employment. In most cases it is only by instilling in the inmate the habit of plain, hard work that any lasting value will be obtained from the expense of imprisoning and training him.
As a part of the replanning of the penitentiary system arising out of the correctional planning committee's report, a special report was prepared on industrial expansion in the
Supply-Justice
present institutions. The objectives were to organize factories with modern methods of production similar to those the inmate would meet in commercial industry, and thus train him for competitive employment and reduce the prospect of his repeating as a criminal. This work, involving a total of approximately 2,000 inmates across Canada, would be done only for the government and tax-supported institutions, and would be sufficiently diversified to have no appreciable effect on any private industry.
To enlist the co-operation of labour and industry on an advisory basis concerning policy, preliminary discussions have taken place during recent months with industrial executives in Toronto and with Mr. Claude Jodoin, president of the Canadian Labour Congress. Reactions have been sympathetic to these proposals, and further discussions are being carried on.
In order to have continuing assistance from industry and labour I propose incorporating into the new draft of the Penitentiary Act a section establishing an advisory committee on penitentiary industry of up to nine members, consisting of representatives chosen from the fields of industry, labour, government and the general public, to advise the commissioner concerning industrial operations to be carried on by inmate labour in connection with the service.
Not only is the inmate encouraged to extend his education and professional training; he is also encouraged to keep in closer contact with his family and those friends who the warden feels will be a good influence upon him in the future. Letter writing restrictions have been substantially lifted, and visits by the family are being given a less clinical treatment. I should mention further that at a number of our institutions we have been able to start a program under which, during the season of certain religious festivals such as Easter and Christmas, relatives of the inmates come to the institution to take part in religious services with inmates and remain there afterward for a social hour in surroundings of complete informality and lack of restraint. During the Easter period just past some 70 relatives attended the Protestant religious services in these circumstances, and an equal number attended the Roman Catholic services.
As one example of the success of these new methods, I might mention the small group of inmates at Kingston penitentiary who during last summer attended night classes at Queen's University to study advanced techniques in the printer's trade. These men mingled freely with other students and were accepted readily by them. Again, you probably heard, Mr. Chairman, of the 14 inmates of the

Supply-Justice
William Head institution who graduated from a public speaking course. Their graduation celebration was held at Victoria, and the function was attended by the mayor of the city and his wife as well as by other civic officials.
I believe that all of Canada-indeed I know that much of the free world-is aware of and interested in our correctional reform program. I have given here a necessarily very much condensed report on progress. While we in the Department of Justice and all the staff of the penitentiaries service are pleased to have been able to record this substantial degree of progress, we realize that much remains to be done. However, I have felt that in asking for continued support for our program by way of these appropriations I should outline to the committee some of the progress made, so the house and the country will know that the money is being put to effective use.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure all the members of the committee have followed closely and with great interest the statement the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) has just made concerning the reform of Canada's penitentiaries.
One of the first aims of such a reform is naturally to facilitate the rehabilitation of the inmates. This rehabilitation process starts within the institution itself but it must keep on after the prisoner has been released. That is one of the objectives the minister mentioned. According to him, we must first arouse in the people of Canada an interest in this reform of our penal institutions and, second, put into practice most of the recommendations contained in the Fauteux report, if not all of them.
In fact, when the Fauteux committee was set up, a few years ago, it was undoubtedly entrusted with the task of making a special study of the situation in the penitentiaries. It completed its task and submitted its report to the government. And now this government is trying to put those recommendations into practice.
In my opinion, one of the most interesting aspects of this question of penitentiaries about which I should like to say a few words, is the inmate's situation when he is freed, and during the period of time between his imprisonment and his full release.
The inmate goes through the various stages the minister mentioned. First, there is the period of maximum security, that is when he is confined to a penitentiary, then the period of medium security and finally that of minimum security, just before his release.
(Mr. Fulton.]
All those stages are most important for the inmates but it is also quite important that the public should know what the inmates go through during those stages.
It is important also that the public be aware of the treatment given to inmates during the medium security period, and more especially during the minimum security period. In fact, it is essential that the public be familiar with the situation of inmates in general after their release, and I believe this is a point that members of the committee should emphasize.
Mr. Chairman, I have here an item published in Le Devoir of November 16, 1960, reporting a statement of the Minister of Justice regarding appointments made, especially at the St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary. I am pleased to point out in particular the appointments of Majors Martineau, Surpre-nant and Desgroseillers, because I had the opportunity of knowing them when I served in the Canadian army. I am convinced that they are worthy of the confidence placed in them and that they will prove equal to their task.
But such was not the purpose of my remarks. I want to stress the importance of the part to be played not by officers and employees of the penitentiaries, but by society in the rehabilitation of inmates.
Mr. Chairman, I now quote from the article I referred to a moment ago:
We are Informed that despite all the good intentions of officials in correctional institutions and their efforts to better prepare inmates to return to a normal and decent life, the apathy of the public and particularly of employers in relation to former inmates remains the greatest obstacle to rehabilitation.
Mr. Chairman, I am sure this article is completely true. We can never repeat often enough to the public at large, and more particularly to employers, that they must try to understand the inmate, a person who through some accident, some misfortune or because he was led into it, has committed a crime but remains an unfortunate human being who would be glad to start a new life in society.
However, if on being released from the penitentiary or from the common prison, the inmate is left to walk the streets, with nothing to do, chances are that he will meet those criminals who traffic in goof balls. In other words, he is bound to get mixed up with bad friends.

Some system must be evolved in order that an inmate will not be left in idleness after his release.
Not only must we reform the penitentiary system as we are doing, but more important, we must reform the individual in society, by understanding the unfortunate situation of the inmate and by contributing to his rehabilitation.

In the last eight or nine months I have been most interested in reading articles about a new policy that is being tried in some places and which, as far as I can ascertain, is working successfully. It does not apply to those who have to be kept under maximum security control, but applies particularly to those under minimum control and perhaps to some extent to those under medium control. It involves inmates who have been sentenced to penitentiary for breaking the law but whose crimes do not involve violence or vicious or malicious actions. The purpose of the policy is to try to keep them in closer touch with society and to aid in their rehabilitation by taking a new approach.
The idea is that after careful study, analysis and scrutiny, those in whom it is felt confidence can be placed should be given the opportunity of working at their own trades under close supervision, of course, outside the walls of the penitentiary. It is my understanding that this policy has been tried, and that in the light of the evidence up to the present time it has proved successful. The person is definitely still a penitentiary inmate. He leaves in the morning, goes to his place of employment and has to return at night. He has to serve his full sentence. Part of the money he earns goes toward his upkeep in the institution to relieve the burden on the taxpayers, and the balance goes for the upkeep of his family so they will be maintained by his own personal work and will not need to become welfare and relief recipients.
I recognize all the difficulties in such a policy, but it must be noted that it is being tried elsewhere and it does seem to have something to recommend it. I am wondering whether any consideration has been given to extending the study of penal reform referred to by the minister into this realm. If consideration has not been given to this idea yet, I believe it is something that might well be studied by the advisory committee which the minister says will be appointed as a result of changes he is recommending in the Penitentiary Act.
I must admit that the articles I have read on the matter intrigue me very much, and if the idea is practicable and applicable it might be a step forward that would assist in certain cases in the rehabilitation of those whom we want to ensure are rehabilitated as quickly as possible and in a proper manner. I would be most interested if the minister would comment on the feasibility and practicability of that suggestion.

I do feel that since the taxpayers' dollars have been spent in making these people pay for their crimes, in trying to rehabilitate them by driving out their antisocial attitudes and giving them a new social conscience, then some provision should be made for assistance of a practical nature when these men are released in order to guarantee that they do not return to crime.

My comments have to do with the application of sections 60, 61 and 62 of the Criminal Code, dealing with habitual criminals. Hon. members know that when an accused has been convicted of three different charges, each punishable by five years or more in the penitentiary, the crown may charge him with being an habitual criminal. I should like the minister, if it is possible, to let us know the number of inmates presently in our penitentiaries who have been convicted of being habitual criminals and are held, au bon plaisir. If a man is sent to the penitentiary for 15, 20 or 25 years, at least there is some limit to his detention.
During the past number of years we have been taking a second look at questions relating to reform and rehabilitation. I do not believe these particular sections of the Criminal Code are in line with our thinking on reform and rehabilitation. I hope the minister will be able to give us a few comments.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE AGAINST REDUCTION OR LOSS OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
I should say, first, that I appreciate very much the remarks of the hon. member for Megantic, with which I thoroughly agree. I have stated on a number of occasions that we might have the best designed program in the world, the best institutions, administered by the best staffs, but this would come to nothing if on release the inmate is unable to find employment. I appreciate the approach of my hon. friend, and I hope his remarks will register with the public and with potential employers.
In so far as the comments of the hon. member for Vancouver East are concerned, he asked me first to consider the possibility of providing what might be called extramural work for inmates as a further step in the program leading toward their ultimate rehabilitation into society. I might tell him that at present we are doing this ourselves, although on what I think might be fairly described as a very limited scale, in connection with pre-release. There are cases in which we arrange for suitable inmates to work outside the walls during the day and return to the institution at night. It is our intention to enlarge this program, but it is definitely part of our program of reform.

My hon. friend will appreciate, however, that you cannot make all these reforms at once. We have in mind the establishment of a pre-release hostel to which selected inmates might be sent, and from which they would go to work in industry in the community- possibly the same job as they may be continuing after their release; that is definitely in our mind.
I should say, of course, that to a certain extent the parole system itself is a step in this direction because an inmate, instead of serving his full sentence in the institution may, if he is regarded by the parole board as suitable, be released from the institution to serve the balance of his sentence outside in employment under the supervision of the parole board. It is, therefore, in a sense quite properly part of the concept which the hon. member for Vancouver East put before us.
I see it is one o'clock, Mr. Chairman, and perhaps I could conclude my reply after lunch.

I have perhaps a somewhat unexpected and unusual way of praising the minister for bringing us so far along this road, because it so happens that I have a filial connection with the report of what I believe was the first penitentiaries commission. This commission reported in 1914 and my father, the late G. M. Macdonnell, was its chairman. That report went a very short way along the road which the minister has taken us infinitely further along.
Perhaps the committee would allow me for just a moment to refer to two or three of the things upon which that commission reported and which would seem far removed from these enlightened days. The commission was set up to inquire into the affairs of the Kingston penitentiary and also, in broad terms, to report on the subject of the conduct and administration of penitentiaries.

Their report into the affairs of the Kingston penitentiary does not make pleasant reading and I shall not take up any of the time of the committee in reading from it. There is just one item to which I would refer. Although it is harsh it has almost an element of ironic humour in it, that when a man was recommended for flogging, as he often was by the sentencing judge on entering the penitentiary, he was flogged on entry and he was also flogged just before he went out. It seems to me there is a bitter irony in flogging a man just before he leaves, because he would certainly not have a very pleasant attitude toward the society which had dealt with him in this way.
The minister had another advantage which I am sure he will not mind my mentioning. That is that he has in his family, in the person of his wife, a trained social worker and I am quite sure that her views also are represented in this legislation.
I would just like to refer to the fact that the commission with which I have, as I say, a filial interest did recommend against flogging; it did recommend schools and hospitals, which apparently were considered quite unnecessary before that day, in penitentiaries; it did recommend that penitentiaries should be operated with a view to encouraging the inhabitants in the habits of order, industry and a better appreciation of the duties of citizenship, and it did recommend that the hosing of convicts and their confinement in a dark cell or dungeon, and shackling them with ball and chain, be abolished.
One other thing was recommended. This was in regard to the employment of prison guards. More regard was to be paid to the character and education of guards with the view that the officials should exercise the best possible influence over the prisoners. There was another recommendation; that in the place of the prison uniform which was worn, a suit and cap of one-tone material, blue or grey, should be adopted.
Perhaps the committee will forgive this little personal excursion. I thought it might be of some interest to other hon. members as well as to myself. It also enables me to say again how far we have come from those rather primitive days and how much we owe to the Minister of Justice for what he has done and is doing.

Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend from Megantic refers to the meeting held in 1958, the occasion of which was to discuss the implementation of the Fauteux committee's report, in which it was obvious there were a number of recommendations which were of mutual federal and provincial concern.
At that time we indicated to the attorneys general of the provinces our readiness to accept in principle the Fauteux committee's recommendation, that we should accept responsibility for the treatment of all prisoners sentenced to terms of over six months. It was as a result of the discussions at that meeting and the conclusions arrived at unanimously that the correctional planning committee was set up, which recommended to us the detailed methods by which we should implement the various recommendations that were then put before us.
Although we agreed in principle at that time on the acceptance of this recommendation to assume responsibility for these additional prisoners, it was made clear to the attorneys general that there was a great deal to be done in the existing federal penitentiary system both from the point of view of reorganizing our system and with regard to improving our own standards before we should be in a position to assume the actual responsibility.
With respect to the first, we have been and are still faced with the problem of overcrowding in our institutions and it would not be reasonable, before we got that under control, to accept responsibility for another 5,000 inmates. In respect to the second, it was recognized in the Robichaud report and the MacDonald committee report, as my hon. friend pointed out, that there are many changes which should be made in our own penal system before we can stand up and say that we have a penal system in operation which is as good as we can make it, or as good as, or better than any in the provinces.
We are anxious to take over this new field when it becomes possible to do so and we are all agreed this should be done in order to provide a better system for prisoners in Canada as a whole, but when the correctional planning committee went into the details of the matter and when we received its report indicating the size of our own problem of reorganization and reform it became only necessary and fair that I should write to the provinces within the last eight or ten months to indicate that I did not expect we should be in a position to go ahead for the next two

or three years. We are pressing on as fast as we can and I hope the report I gave today indicates that substantial progress has been made. I hope that within the next few years we shall be in a position to say to the provinces: we are ready to go ahead and take over the responsibility which was agreed by all that we should assume.

I have listened carefully to the discussion so far, because this is not a field with which I am familiar. I appreciate the forward looking developments which are taking place in our penal institutions, but there are still several questions which I think could profitably be discussed even by an amateur like myself.
In my own limited experience of the working of penitentiaries I have been unfavourably impressed by the number of officers employed in them whose previous experience has been of a military nature. It has often occurred to me that it is not necessary to have persons of this type placed in positions of responsibility in penal institutions. As a result of their military training they are usually not persons inclined to encourage discussion and co-operation; instead, they are inclined to seek direct and complete obedience which is a concept not usually acceptable to the general public-and, of course, prisoners in penitentiaries are still part of the general public. I often have the impression that military discipline only infuriates people and deters them from cooperating. I may not be altogether fair in saying this, but it seems to me that the answers to some of the questions I have put to people with military minds have not been altogether acceptable to me, reflecting, as they did, a type of thinking which was distasteful to me when I was in the service and which still is, now that I am outside it. It seems to me we should give a great deal more consideration to employing people trained in the sociological field rather than those with a background of military training. While it may be all right to give some officers from the armed services jobs in these penitentiaries, I think we should be careful of putting too many of them in this particular field.
I wish to raise another question, one which relates to medical care. It has been brought to my attention that medical care in some of our penitentiaries by no means reaches the standard it should. Looking in the details of the estimates on page 252 I note that for all the penitentiaries we have one medical officer grade II, three medical officers grade I, seven part-time physicians and eight parttime psychiatrists. On the other hand, there are 18 chaplains and one part-time chaplain. It looks as though we look after the spiritual needs of the prisoners much better than we do their medical needs. One particular case at Kingston penitentiary was brought to my attention. The man's sister asked me to go and see him and I did. I received the courtesies that I am sure all hon. members would receive from the staff at the penitentiary if they should happen to go there. I was struck

by the fact that this individual was seen much more often by psychiatrists than by physicians and the reports of the psychiatrists were given more credence than those of the physicians. It seems to me that in an institution as large as Kingston much greater attention should be paid to medical care.
Probably we can all take a lesson from the hon. member for York-Scarborough. He has visited many penitentiaries. A little while ago he said that he had shown interest in a number of them and had gone to visit them. Maybe we should show more interest in these institutions because many things are happening in them that to me are just not right. I have on my desk a return to an order of the house which indicates that a number of people were strapped, and it gives the offences for which they were strapped and the number of strokes they received. In most instances it was because they had talked roughly to an officer. I have a number of returns. I have information on a case that happened in the west. In this case the guard insists he was asked and pratically forced to resign because he raised the question that medical attention was not available to a man who died in solitary confinement. This man had been in solitary confinement previously and at the time of his death was in solitary confinement, with no medical attention available to him. He was completely alone. Of course, I do not know what might have occurred if he had had the medical attention which is normally available in an institution. In this particular case I am told that not even trained nurses were available or anyone who could give first aid, nor was there anyone available who had male nurse training.
It would seem to me that in an institution as large as Kingston, where there are well over 1,000 people, one doctor should be available at all times in the hospital. This means there would have to be three doctors on call. This is not unreasonable. I am sure we would expect this in a little town of 1,000 people. A doctor should be available there at all times. I do not know whether the minister wishes to comment on this particular case. I have read it. It concerns John Bathford, I believe.
The case we are discussing brought to mind the case of Waslychen. I think the minister should comment on this particular case. It is only an indication that all is not as we have been told. No doubt improvements have been made, but improvements remain to be made. There is no reason why we should assume that everything is as it should be. The implications in this particular case bear out what I have said about other cases that have come to my personal attention. This one has been discussed for two or three years.
Supply-Justice
It is a British Columbia case and I do not wish to get involved in it. I have read it. It is the kind of case that warrants an answer. The gentleman should be charged with malicious intent, or something else, because the charges he makes are serious. I do not think it should be just left in the air. It should be answered and then some improvement made in the situation which would prevent it happening again, or it should be shown that the individual is not correct in the charges he makes. This case has been widely aired on the radio. I have read copies of the radio scripts and articles in the newspapers. It is a very well-known case.
I should like to bring another problem to the attention of the minister. This is an old one. I should like to read from the prisoners' own magazine entitled C.B. Diamond, dated October-November, 1959, Kingston penitentiary. I turn to page 24 of the magazine where we find the following:
Canada v. Russia Prison systems and visits The Russian system:
(The following is an excerpt from an article which appeared in Life magazine and was written by Judge Samuel Leibowitz, a prominent American jurist after a recent trip through the Soviet union.)
One other feature impressed me rather profoundly while I was inspecting Krukovd (the name of the prison). During my unconducted tour I strolled into a building which contained a series of small bedrooms. I glanced into one. A man and woman were sitting on a bed, engrossed in conversation.
"You don't have regular visiting rooms?" I (Mr. Leibowitz) asked the general. I was thinking of the many iron-cage interview rooms I have seen in the U.S., where a prisoner is permitted 30 minutes conversation with his wife perhaps once a month through a screen and under the eyes of guards.
