I continue:
General Bochkov looked at me in surprise. "No," he said. "Our method is what you see here. This is a prisoner being visited by his wife, who will live with him several days. She was brought here at government expense and can come once a month, as long as his conduct is good. It is one of the reasons, I think, why we have so few efforts at escape.
Your prison methods in America disregard a prisoner's sexual and emotional life. It is part of your vengeful attitude. You feel it is none of your concern what happens to his marriage, to his wife, to the normal sex drive, to the most powerful instinct he has.
Don't think we don't know what goes on under your system. In your country a prisoner's marriage often disintegrates, robbing him of a central motive for reform. At best he is torn by doubts about his wife's virtue during the years they are separated and he may very likely be plunged into despair by learning that legally or otherwise

Supply-Justice
she has forsaken him. And homosexuality, of course, is one of the biggest headaches of the wardens in your institutions."
The Canadian system:	(As practised at Collin's
bay Penitentiary).
The iron-cage system is not used at Collin's bay. There is no physical barrier between visitors and inmates, but the rules demand that there be absolutely no physical contact. No handshake between a father or brother .. . No wifely kiss ... No kiss between mother and son ... Nothing. The rules are strictly observed here. The other day I was visiting with my parents at the same time as another inmate was being visited by his wife. The half-hour period that we are allowed once a month came to an end and this man's wife leaned over to kiss him goodbye. It was a visible struggle for him to turn away as he must do, or else lose his visiting privileges. The disappointment in his wife's eyes also was plain. She did not understand why. She was hurt and the visit most certainly left her feeling depressed. That made the inmate feel even worse than if she had not come to see him. He felt so helpless: not able to comfort his wife when she needed it most.
One-half of an hour a month, that is all that is allowed for an inmate to try to keep his family together. And then just with conversation.
The article goes on to talk about the children coming. When I was at Kingston one could talk to one of the prisoners, but I had no desire to have a private conversation with one of them. One is aware of the fact that the guard is within hearing distance, and I do know that this must put a strain on the families. Unless something has happened in the past to make the present system at Kingston necessary, I think we should be developing a much more humane method of operation. I have referred to this prisoner's view of what he would like to see done and from my experience I am certainly in complete agreement with him. I can see no reason why we cannot find a much better method of dealing with this problem. It will be solved to some extent, of course, when we get away from enclosed prisons to the open-door type. As long as the prison building at Kingston remains where it is, it seems to me that we will always attempt to make use of it but in doing so we are actually making use of something that belongs in the decades of past centuries because of the nature of the building and the type of prison it is.
I have known people who have come out of Kingston penitentiary to resume civilian life, if that is what you call it, expecting to resume their married life only to experience a strained relationships not because of the wife's infidelity but because of the husband suspecting infidelity. The present system does nothing to make the return of the prisoner to civilian life that much easier.
This prisoner to whom I have referred suggests a different system and has quoted Judge Samuel Liebowitz as saying that it is not an unreasonable one. There should be no reason why arrangements could not be made at Kingston penitentiary so that wives

and families could spend some time alone with their husbands and fathers. I may be wrong because of my inexperience in this field and the fact that I have not taken the interest I probably should have but it seems to me that something should be done that would be much more satisfactory than the present cold-blooded system.
I asked the guard the other day what his point was in listening to the conversation and he said he had no particular reasons except that it was his job to do so. He said he was supposed to listen to the conversation. I had no objection to him listening to my conversation but if I were in that prison and my wife came to visit me I think I would object violently to him listening to our conservation. I think we should move quickly to do something about these problems that are inherent in the very type of building at Kingston. This massive rock pile at Kingston is probably only good for the use to which it is being put. We should be working very hard to eliminate that prison.
While it is true that there are prisoners of the type to which the minister refers who may be put into solitary confinement possibly at their own request, it seems to me that we have failed to find a better way of solving the problem. I should like to refer to the answer to question 172 asked by the hon. member for Skeena on April 11, 1961. It has been mentioned that there are two prisoners who have been in solitary confinement for six years, 200 days and four years, 197 days, respectively but there are many who are in confinement for disciplinary reasons or under regulation 69, whatever that may be. For example, I note from the figures given here that various prisoners have been in solitary confinement for 208 days, 70 days, 128 days, 104 days, 244 days, 263 days, 109 days, and so on. There are many of these cases where prisoners are in solitary confinement for a considerable length of time and it seems to me that this is rather an archaic way of dealing with the problem. They might as well be punished by being placed in stocks in front of the town hall.
Obviously this system has not worked with many of these men. Men have not only been confined just for 21 days but many have been confined for close to a year, and the result has not been satisfactory. Such punishment can be inflicted as often as you want to inflict it and probably it is not too much of a hardship on these men. It seems to me that a great deal remains to be done and it behooves members of parliament to become more interested in the matter.
It has always seemed to me that to be too interested in our penitentiaries has been regarded as a nasty business. It might be

very nice to look the other way but when you make inquiries and offer suggestions and are given the brush-off it obviously behooves you to do something about it. The whole matter needs to be investigated further from the point of view of the institution and it needs more study on the part of members because their knowledge is not sufficient to understand the needs of the institution.
I have referred to the matter of prisoners in Kingston who have wives and young children and 1 see absolutely no reason why a prisoner could not be put in a room with his wife and children in order to talk to them privately. They cannot get out the door because it is bolted. What do you expect they are going to do? The children are not going to run away. They could be held as hostages. It seems to me that the present method is archaic.
I do not know whether we have advanced enough socially in this country to use the Russian system. Certainly the Americans have been using it for many years in the more advanced states. There are also some states that are much more in the dark ages than we are. However, there are some states that use this visiting technique. Cottages are provided and the family can come and stay for the week end. How much better it is for people who are going back into society to have a close relationship with that society particularly after they have been confined for a number of years. Otherwise it seems to me we are asking for trouble when we throw them out into society. They go back to families who have grown away from them and they do not know them any more. We are not doing them any favour and this in turn in reflected in their attitude to society.
The matter of medical attention is one that I think we should consider. It may be quite true that prisoners are probably just as good at swinging the lead as army people. This may be one of the reasons why they are not dealt with too favourably. A number of people in the penitentiaries division were army officers and they deal with these matters in that light. It does seem to me that, medically speaking, the penitentiaries are much understaffed. Possibly they are overstaffed in a psychiatric and psychological sense. In any event, it seems to me that something should be done to correct the situation.
I would think that part of the problem could be met simply by having doctors come to the penitentiaries as consultants. In that way there would at least be some assurance of impartiality. If there is only one doctor in Kingston penitentiary and he is dealing with 1,400 or 1,500 people, I am quite sure there are some who would say that the doctor is no good, that the doctor is a quack and not
Supply-J ustice
competent because the same thing occurs in every little town. You may even disagree with your wife on this matter. She may go to one doctor and you may go to another. You have faith in your doctor and she has faith in hers. However, it seems to me that with such a large number of inmates in our prisons there should be some opportunity for them to have some choice. When cases such as the Waslychen case are brought to the attention of the minister, I think there is need to give consideration to the situation which I in my limited experience have also found to exist. I hope the minister will give some consideration to the problems of the prisoners themselves in connection with this matter of being able to visit with their families.

speechtext: I rise, Mr. Chairman, merely for the purpose of putting in what lawyers call a caveat to the remarks made by the hon. member for Timiskaming. I am sure his representations will be considered on their merits by the minister and his staff. The point upon which I do wish to put in a caveat is this: The member seems to wash out, as unsuitable for positions on the penitentiary staff, military officers. I should like to differ with him there. In my opinion, a regimental officer who has shared the toils and dangers of battle with his men is much more competent to deal in a humane and understanding way with the ordinary, run of the mill citizens we come across both inside and outside penitentiaries.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE AGAINST REDUCTION OR LOSS OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
The hon. member for Timiskaming has, unfortunately, concerned himself primarily with situations and circumstances going back as far as five years. I think if he would concern himself more with what the situation is today, he would not have such a gloomy, pessimistic view of the situation in our penitentiaries as he seems to have.
In so far as the case in British Columbia is concerned, he is talking about events that took place in 1958, and he is not even talking accurately about them. The inmate in question who died was seen every day by the orderly from the prison hospital, and every two or three days by the prison medical doctor. It is quite true that this case and others brought to my attention, after having been investigated by members of the correctional planning committee the chairman of which is now the commissioner for penitentiaries, led me to the conclusion there was an unsatisfactory situation in the British Columbia penitentiary. Action was taken to remedy the situation in

Supply-Justice
the prison hospital and to have medical service available. I am only sorry that the hon. member, who professes such a desire to visit our penitentiaries and obtain up to date information, has not visited British Columbia to satisfy himself as to the present circumstances.
It might interest the hon. member also to know that we have a substantial provision in the main estimates this year for commencing the construction of a 50 bed hospital at Kingston penitentiary. It is quite true that we will probably never be able to have as many doctors serving the penitentiaries as we might think ideal in order to provide adequate medical service. I am satisfied, however, that if my hon. friend will visit any one of our institutions he will find the situation has improved appreciably over what it was in the past.
We are embarking upon a new system which we have instituted in at least two of our penitentiaries, that is arranging contracts with clinics to provide service instead of relying exclusively on the employment of one doctor to whom we can rarely pay a salary under the appropriations authorized here. No first class man is prepared to give his whole time to the penitentiary. Under the contract system, we are getting very good service, and that is the system which we have instituted in British Columbia, starting about a year ago.
In so far as conditions prevailing with respect to visitors to institutions are concerned, I was interested to note that my hon. friend again was reading from a publication dated October or November, 1959, going back about two years. I am not saying that the situation in every one of our institutions is satisfactory today, but it is certainly vastly improved over what it was two or three years ago. My hon. friend went on to refer to the situation in Kingston, where he is dealing with an overcrowded maximum security institution. I have never hesitated to admit that conditions at Kingston and St. Vincent de Paul, particularly these two institutions, are unsatisfactory because of the gross overcrowding there.
My hon. friend has picked out, as he is entitled to do if he wants, one of our overcrowded, maximum security institutions where certain security difficulties are necessarily encountered and impose limitations on doing the things we would like to do to improve visiting facilities. If he were to go to some of our medium security institutions or other maximum security institutions, he would see a decided change. I mentioned in my introductory remarks a new approach to visiting and letter writing, as well as the fact that inmates spend time out of their

cells in communal activities. Visiting privileges are but one part of the new approach to our penitentiaries program. Naturally enough, we have been making the most progress in those institutions where the physical set-up enables this to be done. As soon as we can get other new institutions in Ontario to relieve the overcrowded situation in Kingston, then there will be some progress because of the physical facilities available. The raising of the limitation on the number of visits authorized per inmate at Kingston would mean that some inmates would have frequent visitors, while others would have none. We have to ration them, unfortunately, because of the limitation of physical accommodation we have for visitors.

We are not really disagreeing with each other. I said I was only aware of and concerned with Kingston. However, I believe the minister is unfair in his treatment of this other matter when he says I am raising a matter that is three years old. I was reading from a copy of an interview that took place at 6.10 p.m. on Wednesday, March 15, 1961. A question was asked about it by the hon. member for Skeena on the 17th, and the minister's reply does not appear to me to be valid at all. This condition has existed for three years and charges have been made and are still being made about it.
The minister also referred to the fact that in this particular hospital in British Columbia there were nurses. In a broadcast by Jack Webster during the program called "City Mike", on April 6, 1960, this statement was made:
The male nurses at the pen are not registered nurses. They are graduates of Essondale nursing hospital-psychiatric nurses. They do hold first aid certificates.
I am also aware of the fact that the doctors should be allowed to operate their own practice. It was for this reason I suggested that doctors should be on a 24-hour basis, having three doctors rather than one so that one doctor would be in attendance at all times and yet these doctors would still be able to operate their own practice to supplement their income. It is true that a good doctor is not going to work for the penitentiaries branch at $7,000 per annum when he can make $18,000 to $20,000 in private practice. We are aware of these things, but this does not mean that we can justify the circumstances and nothing should be done about them.
I am aware of the improvement that has been made at Joyceville, but it would take a great many of these little prisons to equal one Kingston penitentiary in which there are 1,200 or 1,500 inmates. It takes a great many of these little institutions like that at Joyceville and at the new farm that is going in

there at Kingston to make up the number of people who are in Kingston penitentiary. As to the matter that was raised and the problem involved in it, maybe the minister did not understand. I did not intend to go into it. I did not want to do so and I am not going to do it now. I think some of the members from British Columbia have been much more interested in it than have I.
However, there is an implication with regard to one of the guards, a man who had served with the minister in the armed services or who had served under him, a man who has had service in many parts of the world under several of the officers who are now members of the House of Commons, and I presume they personally know whether or not he is honest. The implication is that he has been fired or at least has been forced to resign, or says he has been forced to resign, because he went to the minister, went over the heads of the penitentiary branch and particularly the officials in British Columbia. He says that this is why he had to resign.
What the minister indicates is this, and I do not disagree because what he says is borne out by all the information that I have. The minister indicates that he had an investigation into the hospital, that he was unsatisfied with the situation existing and that he corrected this situation. However, we still have this gentleman who appears still to want to work in the penitentiary department and who says he was fired or was forced to resign. He points out some of the disciplinary action that was taken against him because he went to the minister.
I also should like to say that this argument fits in very much with the argument that I was making against the military people who sometimes are involved. I have no disagreement with what was said by the hon. member for Greenwood. I agree that the training in many cases is the best training that could possibly be given. In other cases there is a tendency to follow the book and not to give any consideration to the exceptions that sometimes make up the rule. It is for these reasons that I mentioned this particular case. The minister himself is going to have to justify to himself-because he knows much more about it than does anyone else-if this is so, the reason why this happened.
I am concerned only for this reason. It would mean that if anybody wanted to make any suggestion or wanted to bring to the attention of the minister any malpractice that was taking place he would be immediately, as Mr. Bathford indicates punished in the same way and his dismissal or his resignation would be sought in the same manner. If this is true, I think the minister will 90205-6-386

agree with me that it would eliminate part of the protection or control that the whole system would have by having a co-operative staff. I may be tempering all this on something else. I could point out that this happened in a local provincial jail where the situation was very much the same and where eventually an investigation in Ontario into the situation resulted in the firing of a warden and the top executives in that prison. However, it did not get back the jobs of the people who brought this matter to the attention of the attorney general in the first place. It is perhaps unfortunate that the hon. member does not put on the record all the other information he has available in connection with this case. It was also given earlier in this House of Commons in answer to questions by the hon. member for Skeena. It is true that the guard in question was one of those who brought to the attention of the authorities and ultimately to my attention directly, through a member of my staff, what he regarded as the unsatisfactory situation with respect to the hospital and medical facilities in British Columbia penitentiary. As I have indicated, that situation was investigated and effective steps were taken to improve the situation. The penitentiary officer in question was not proceeded against or adversely reported upon in any way as a result of the fact that he had brought this information to my attention. In the course of the reorganization of our penitentiary service as a whole the then warden of British Columbia penitentiary was transferred to Saskatchewan penitentiary. When the new warden arrived in British Columbia, in the course of his review of the personnel serving under him, he recommended that an annual salary increase, which had been withheld from the guard in question, should in fact be authorized and be made retroactive. That was the treatment this guard received and it is far from being treatment prejudiced to his situation. The new warden indeed preferred him and went out of his way to recommend that a retroactive adjustment in his favour should be made and that was accomplished and instituted by the new commissioner.
This is far from being suggestive of the fact that the guard was being prejudiced and persecuted because of the initiative he had taken. Some time later however, he himself submitted his resignation. His resignation

Supply-Justice
was accepted and forwarded. He came forward himself later and said that he wanted the opportunity of stating his reasons. He was invited to state his reasons and was informed that, as the regulations provided, they would be forwarded to the commissioner. Afterwards he wrote a letter saying that, under the circumstances, he had decided that he did not wish to submit any reasons for his resignation.
I think it is unfortunate that my hon. friend did not put that information on the record because it is all in his possession. It indicates the very contrary of what he has been trying to establish, namely that this guard was prejudiced and persecuted because he brought information to my attention.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to take this opportunity to wish the minister well in his program. I fully realize that he has a problem which is serious all over the country at the present time and I should like to congratulate him on the progress that has been made.
I should also like to answer the hon. member for Timiskaming. I think if these people want to stay with their families, all they have to do is keep out of trouble.
The hon. member said there are not enough medical practitioners in the penitentiaries. There are many places in British Columbia with 1,500 or 2,000 inhabitants which have no medical practitioners at all, and I think they should be given consideration.
I should like to review under this item the request I have made in the past. First I should like to refer to my remarks in 1958 when I asked for the establishment of a minimum security prison or institution in the Fernie area. I said:
The establishment in Fernie of a penitentiary would have the effect of bringing people into the area and providing the personnel of the penitentiary with an attractive community in which to reside.
The minister's reply at that time was as follows:
We will have to survey the whole available field and, in fairness, I think I must say that when we make a decision it will have to be made in accordance with what seems to be the best program of building that we can devise.
In 1959 I also raised the same question on the floor of the house and at that time I said:
-I should like to add my recommendation to those already made for proposed construction of penitentiaries in western Canada.
In fact, we will be very pleased to receive anything that is available. I said at that time:
At the moment I am not very interested in the type of construction, but I am interested in the location. We have already established a precedent in the establishment and construction of a penitentiary at Springhill.

The minister replied:
When we get the committee's report we shall be able to come to some final conclusion. As I have assured my hon. friend and others who have written me on behalf of Fernie on previous occasions, the suitability of that location will be most carefully investigated.
In 1960 also I raised this same matter and asked approximately the same question. I said:
Ever since being elected to this house in March, 1958 I have been quite interested in the construction of penitentiaries in western Canada. We have placed our views before the department with regard to the need for penitentiaries in British Columbia. We have requested also that serious consideration be given to locating a penitentiary in the city of Fernie.
At that time the minister replied:
-I would remind the committee that we are designing a national system of correctional institutions. The program we are developing will be nation wide and the new institutions, wherever and whenever built, have to fit in with the national plan.
In addition to that, Mr. Chairman, we have the request for penitentiaries in other places. I notice that since the trouble with the mines at Springhill-and the situation is very similar in my own constituency-there has been a development in the penitentiary system. I have here an editorial headed:
Good old Elliot Lake.
This editorial appeared in the Fernie Free Press on July 7, 1960:
In another part of this issue will be found a news story from Elliot Lake, Ontario, which is threatened with the closure of some uranium mines. It reads in part: "Plans for a $2 million prison farm and a provincial park development to bolster the economy of this slump-threatened centre were announced-
We have this progress in other places, and we have the same situation in Fernie. I believe that some action should be taken. It has been a year and a half now since the committee submitted its report on this matter; it was submitted a year ago last January. I feel that our committee did a wonderful job on this report and some action should now be forthcoming.
I have not seen the press report myself and I cannot quote it, but I understand the minister made a statement concerning the system of minimum security prisons and forestry camps running from Ontario through to Prince Albert, Saskatchewan. We have seen the same thing in British Columbia; minimum security institutions and forestry camps have spread as far as the lower mainland in the Okanagan.
I realize the terrific problem the minister has on his hands at the present time, but I feel that now is the time to make a change in this policy. I do not feel this is a time

I think this is the start of the R.C.M.P. items. I did indicate I would be prepared to make a statement at this point. It will not be of any great length, so the hon. member for Kootenay West will not have to defer his remarks very long if he will be good enough to allow me to make it now.
At the outset of our consideration of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police estimates for the present fiscal year, I should like to take the opportunity to say a few words to this committee about one of the activities or functions of the force which has recently been the subject of some comment. I refer to the security work which has been the responsibility of the force for many years and which has been performed unobtrusively, efficiently and with the least possible interference with the private lives of Canadian citizens.
It is, I am certain, obvious to all members of this committee, as it is to the public of Canada, that a security and intelligence service is necessary in order to preserve national security in the present world situation. This is not something which gives either the government or the members of the R.C.M.P. any pleasure or satisfaction, but it is, in our view, a fact arising from the situation in the world today, and as a result the task of carrying out this work is imposed upon the R.C.M.P. They have not asked for it. They do not particularly relish it, but I do venture to say that they carry it out in a manner which is most satisfactory to the Canadian public. It is not the kind of work which can be carried out without giving rise to misgivings and occasional unpleasant situations, but I think I should remind the committee that one or to unpleasant incidents will attract attention out of all proportion to the relation they bear to the total amount of activity in which the security force is engaged. Of the many thousands of inquiries made it is only a fraction of 1 per cent that gives rise to these difficulties and the publicity which occasionally occurs. I should like also to mention that in the security field the function of the R.C.M.P. is to gather facts and not to pass judgment on those facts. That responsibility rests elsewhere, primarily with the government. Others are responsible for judging the facts and deciding what should be done in view of the facts so reported.
Some of the things I have said are perhaps a little obvious but in view of the comments

I have seen, which suggest a misunderstanding, it might not hurt to repeat them. Obviously a security and intelligence service which does not keep its information secret, confidential and withheld from unauthorized persons is not fulfilling its responsibility. We get criticism on two counts. The R.C.M.P. are criticized because they keep their information confidential and refuse to disclose it. On the other hand there have been criticisms because, it is said, the fact that they are making these investigations known, whereas it should have been kept secret. Any security service must maintain its information absolutely confidential, for the use only of those who are authorized to receive it. It would be unfortunate indeed if the security program were to involve unnecessary interference with the private lives of Canadian citizens. Not only would this be undesirable from the individual's point of view, but it would injure the security program itself by reducing public support for the program, a support that is so necessary.
I am satisfied that I do not need to spend any time reminding members of this committee that there is a need for a security and intelligence service to protect the interest of Canada and Canadians against the efforts of those who are our opponents and who resort to espionage and subversive efforts to pursue and gain their own end. It is because of this that we have a security service. I know also that all hon. members are concerned that our security program should not cause any undue or unnecessary inconvenience to any Canadian citizen. I share this concern and I assure the committee that this matter is receiving and will continue to receive my personal attention as it does that of the commissioner and of all responsible officers of the R.C.M. police.
As I said, we know we cannot give 100 per cent satisfaction in this field. We know that we shall never have the Utopia in which this kind of activity on our part is unnecessary and which will not give rise to occasional concern. We know that the job is necessary. It is being done efficiently and we anticipate that it will have the over-all support of the Canadian people so long as we are scrupulous, as we are, to see that it is carried out with the minimum possible interference with the private lives and concerns of individuals; in other words, as far as it is humanly possible to ensure it, no individual is going to be unjustly prejudiced as a result of the application of this policy on the one hand. On the other it is a responsibility which neither the R.C.M. police, which has always accepted its responsibilities, nor the government, which has the over-all responsibility for the national interests, can avoid.

Mr. Chairman, I am very glad indeed that the minister opened the study of this item by saying a few words on security. As a matter of fact, this is the topic that I was concerned with and I should like to make a few remarks on it. There is no doubt that the task of security work is very important indeed, and there is also no doubt in my mind that even if the members of the R.C.M. Police who are engaged in this work are doing their utmost to discharge their duties efficiently, there is room for improvement. This is evidenced, I think, by at least three things. The first one that comes to my mind is, of course, the Biernacki case in Montreal. I do not want to deal with it because it is before the courts.
The other case that comes to mind is in the province of Quebec also and arose in Laval University where two students were under inquiry. The third thing which prompts me to say there is room for improvement is the annual report of the R.C.M. police for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1960.
This report shows that only two members of the force were sent on cipher training courses; only nine took language training courses, which would surely be needed for comprehensive security work; three were taking full-time university training last year, and only one graduated in law in 1959-60. Two were studying for an arts degree and 12 members of the force were taking a 1-year non-degree university course.
According to the report, it is a fact that 54 members of the R.C.M. Police were undertaking or about to complete their training in security and intelligence. These figures appear on pages 43 and 44 of the report.
I am also informed, Mr. Chairman, and I have no reason to believe that my information is not correct, that at the present time the basic schooling requirement for entrance into the R.C.M. police is only grade 10. I would think that a much higher grade should be required, especially for the members of the force engaged in security work. I am sure the minister will agree with me that to carry on detective work in this field of security requires a vast knowledge of political theory in order to investigate security matters and also to conduct investigations. Of course, I do not know exactly what kind of course is envisaged in security and intelligence work and I hope the minister will give us some details on that.
I should like to put some questions to the minister which he might answer a little later on. How many constables in the security division have only the minimum entrance requirement of grade 10? How many N.C.O.'s or commissioned officers have only grade 10 education or instruction? At the same time

Supply-Justice
the minister might explain to us why only nine members of the force took language training. Why are only three studying for a full law degree and only two for an arts degree? The minister might also tell the committee, perhaps not in a detailed way, how much it would cost to require every security investigator to have a degree in political and sociological sciences.
I mentioned the case of the two students in Laval University who were investigated. The minister might tell the committee if some matters other than communism are grounds for investigation. I would mention especially some groups in Canada that are advocating that the United States take over Canada, or those who are advocating the separation of Quebec from the rest of Canada. Are these also the subject of investigation?
These are the remarks that I wanted to put on the record at this time. In answering I hope the minister will let us know what kind of courses are required for security and intelligence investigators and why only those that I have mentioned are studying for degrees in law and the arts?

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the minister's remarks with respect to the question of security investigations and I shall deal with that question a little later on. However, before doing so, I wish to express my sincere appreciation of the history, of the traditions, of the record and of the services performed by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, sometimes under very difficult circumstances. I must say the force has quite an unusual and difficult service to perform in the constituency which I have the honour to represent. I have known a number of the inspectors, officers, N.C.O.'s and men in the force, and have known some for a number of years. I must say they are most patient and most careful in the exercise of their duties, very frustrating and difficult duties at times, to make certain that they carry them out in accord with their traditions and our usual practices.
I am particularly impressed with the community work undertaken by members of the force in the district which I know best, namely the Kootenays. It usually takes the form of three types of activity. First, there is their interest, which is very much appreciated in the smaller communities, in community activities and organizations. I have had a number of people comment on this and I know all these small communities quite well indeed. I think this is a very good example of the excellent training and discipline the force receives because when you have one, two or three members of the force in an isolated detachment it is very easy,

human beings being what they are, not to do more than is required in the line of duty.
The second type of activity is co-operation with local organizations in the recognition of days of national importance. This has been very much appreciated, particularly with respect to remembrance day because in a number of the larger places they put themselves out to help to make the day successful in the proper sense of the word.
Third, there is the work of a number of corporals and constables in connection with youth groups which I think is of particular importance. I am thinking of members of three or four detachments in my constituency who are interested in church work, in scouts and other youth groups, and I find that this is a most valuable activity on the part of members of the force. In the small communities, particularly where the population is not large, these men have an influence out of all proportion to their numbers compared with the personal influence a person can exercise in a very large centre. I have talked to a number of young people in these places and I can say that this work on their part, which is quite beyond the call of their normal duties, is appreciated by the parents and particularly by the boys in question who, because of this contact with members of the force, have a respect for them as representatives of the state interested in the preservation of the rights and privileges that we should all enjoy.
Having said that, I must say that I have been asked to deal with a matter this afternoon that has concerned quite a number of people. I have had a lady visit me as the representative of the council of students at Laval University and have had persons converse with me from Queen's University and from the University of Toronto. This matter has to do with some aspects of the activities of the security section of the force which have been brought to the attention of the public recently through the press. I refer to the same circumstances that were mentioned by the previous speaker.
If I understood the minister correctly, the security force does its best to perform its duties without trespassing upon the rights of citizens, and I think this is generally true. But the parliament of Canada is the place to raise any question that arises when, in the opinion of some persons, there has been a transgression of their human rights and fundamental freedoms. I have promised a number of persons to raise this matter on these estimates, which is the appropriate time.
I want to refer first of all to an article that appeared in La Presse of Montreal on Tuesday, May 23. I had the article translated

by the bureau of translation so I presume it is accurate. It is entitled "Sequel to an Article from Le Carabin; If You Do Not Like the Atom Bomb, Beware the R.C.M.P." The article is written by Jean David. I am going to read it and comment on it as I do so because, as the previous speaker said, I think it indicates clearly that possibly there is some need for improvement and for greater care under particular circumstances. I am quite sure that no member of the house would question the necessity for security forces or that their work is necessary. What we are concerned about is that the security force should carry on according to the traditions of the force and according to the accepted understanding of the rights and privileges of the citizens of this country. I read:
Is a person suspect because he is against nuclear armaments? "We must protect life and property", is the answer you will get from a Mr. Berlinguette. This man is said to be the chief of the counterespionage section of the Quebec detachment of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
That is the answer Mr. Berlinguette gave to two Laval students who came to inquire about an investigation being made of them. An R.C.M.P. constable by the name of Plourde had called them communists" in the presence of a female student whom he was asking to do espionage for the Mounted Police.
I might say that I asked the young lady who came from Quebec city to visit me if this was correct and she said the student council would vouch that this was an accurate report of the circumstances of the case. I come to the next paragraph headed "Origin of the Affair". It reads as follows:
The affair began with the publication of two pages of articles against nuclear weapons in Le Carabin, a students' newspaper at Laval, edition of April 20. The action was taken by the Laval section of the intervarsity campaign for nuclear disarmament. Miss Helene Senecal and Mr. Edward Smith set the pages and wrote a preamble. Among the various texts compiled by the two students are a quotation by Nikita Khrushchev himself, but also testimonies from persons as Catholic as Pope Pius XII and John F. Kennedy. What is more laughable in the context is the inclusion of a short poem by Ezra Pound, who is well known for his fascist sympathies.
One week after this issue of the Carabin appeared, an officer of the Mounted Police by the name of Plourde approached Miss Jacqueline Cyr, a student in pedagogy and guidance as a "friend of the family". Officer Plourde told the girl that he was making an investigation of communism at Laval. When she asked him what was the matter, Plourde talked to her about the intervarsity campaign for nuclear disarmament. He thrust under her nose, the two pages from the Carabin produced by Helene Senecal and Edward Smith.
If that report is accurate it does indicate that there is need for some improvement because it is quite obvious that this officer or constable was not carrying out security work in the proper manner. I continue:

Officer Plourde then asked Miss Cyr to join the group and report to him on the activities of the section. He appealed to her patriotism, pointing out that her co-operation would be greatly appreciated by the R.C.M.P. Jacqueline Cyr did not agree to join the game, and what is more, she expressed her support for the I.V.C.N.D., and also attacked Plourde and his methods. Previously, Officer Plourde had questioned her at length about the two persons who were responsible for the pages in the Carabin. She had objected to that interrogation. As he left her, Plourde did not conceal his exasperation.
Meanwhile, a Mr. Jean Marc Bourdet was ostentatiously making an investigation of the two students. Bourdet introduced himself as a counterespionage agent. The mounted police told the students that they did not know that man and also repeated it to us. Irritated by these methods, Helene Senecal and Edward Smith decided to take the bull by the horns. They telephoned the R.C.M.P. and demanded explanations. An officer replied that the R.C.M.P. would get in touch with them. They waited. A week passed. Despite the fact that it was examination time, they telephoned again. Once again an attempt was made to brush them off, but they insisted. Finally they were told that it was not a question that could be settled over the telephone and were asked to report to the headquarters. An appointment was made for them.	.
Therefore on May 8, between two examinations, the two students proceeded to No. 1 Grande Allee east. Miss Senecal asked to speak to the chief of the counter-espionage section. The receptionist replied, "Counter-espionage? We don't have that here." Miss Senecal then replied that they had an appointment with someone in any case. The receptionist asked them to be seated.
This is a report of the interview.
After a few minutes a man came down from the first floor and took them up to his office. On the door were the words "Criminal Investigations". The man never revealed his name or position. However, Helene Senecal deciphered the name Berlinguette which was on a plaque; she could only see the tops of the letters and she had to read them upside down. (Actually, after several calls to the mounted police, Quebec detachment and Montreal detachment, we managed to confirm that there is an officer by that name and that his initials are J. F. We have never been able to learn the initials of officer Plourde, but we were assured that an officer by that name is with the Quebec detachment).
Then followed a strange dialogue. Let us introduce the actors. We have told all we know about officer J. F. Berlinguette. Edward Smith is a young American from Lynn, Massachusetts; he has just completed his 2nd year in social work at Laval. Helene Senecal is the daughter of a well known lawyer on St. James street. After studies at Marianopolis, she went last September to the faculty of social science at Laval.
Officer Berlinguette first congratulated the two students for having come to see him in connection with this affair before he called them. But in a few minutes he told them that he did not know at all what they were talking about.
Berlinguette admitted moreover that Plourde got in touch with Miss Cyr, but cast doubt on the girl's evidence. He denied that Plourde asked Jacqueline Cyr to do spying. Each time he was pressed by the two students, Berlinguette answered something like this: "That little girl got excited and it is very easy to alter the facts." He repeated such a phrase several times.

Supply-J ustice
At one moment the officer told the students that he knew perfectly well they were not communists, that the I.V.C.N.D. is not a commumst organization and added that the mounted police is interested only in "communist infiltration". But although he insisted and repeated that the two students were not the subject of any investigation, he forgot himself later and gave to understand that he knew Smith was an American. Smith asked him how he knew. Berlinguette told him that there are not many English-speaking students at Laval and that he knows them all.
At another moment he said that he had investigated the persons responsible for the two pages in question "because I had orders to investigate". From whom? It is not known.
Later this man who had said a few minutes earlier that there had not been any investigation declared this time with regard to Miss Cyr, "The next time an investigation is made, we will try to find someone more reliable than that".
That is, to spy on her fellow students.
The two young people then pointed out that the premier of Saskatchewan, Mr. Tommy Douglas, had attacked the mounted police the day before for an investigation it allegedly made of the national committee against the dangers of radioactivity. Berlinguette did not conceal the slight importance he attaches to the C.C.F. leader and suggested that by such a statement he had a political objective in mind. With regard to the national committee against dangers of radioactivity Berlinguette first maintained that the R.C.M.P. has never made an investigation of that organization (it is known that, for example, one of the directors of the Montreal section is Father Jacques Cousi-neau, S.J.). A few minutes later Berlinguette went on to say that if the R.C.M.P. made an investigation of the committee in question it was not because of its communist activities, but because there exists "a danger of communist infiltration in such organizations".
In reply to the students who attacked the methods of the R.C.M.P., officer Berlinguette said, "We must protect life and property." And he went on, "Who knows how many members of the clergy are communists? Who knows how many people in the Conservative party, in the Liberal party are communists."
You will note, Mr. Chairman, he did not mention this little group over here. I mention this report to indicate the ridiculous nature of these comments by a person engaged in security work.
He even added, "We know very well that Jean Lesage is not a communist, but who is to say that there are not some people in his party who are communists?"
Berlinguette also had this to say to Helene Senecal and Edward Smith concerning their fellow students in the I.V.C.N.D. whose ideas the young people said they knew: "But what do you know about that? You did not know them until one or two years ago. What did they do before? Where do they come from?"
The two young people then asked Berlinguette if the R.C.M.P., by such an "investigation" did not wish simply to discredit an organization such as the I.V.C.N.D., by sowing seeds of doubt. Berlinguette did not refute that statement, even though he admitted that there was nothing communistic about the organization. But he stressed the idea of "communist infiltration", and repeated one of his favourite phrases "We must protect life and property".

Closing word: Officer Berlinguette told the two young people, "We have no apologies to make to you."
The interview lasted about three quarters of an hour.
I place this report on record in full to indicate support for the previous hon. member who suggested that some of these people have not the qualifications required to carry out this sort of work with discretion and without offence to people. As I said, I have discussed this question very carefully with the representatives of the students council of Laval University, with a number of people. Members of the faculty of universities and students in a number of cities are concerned. A great number of people are concerned and aroused by this newspaper report which, apparently, is news right across Canada. I am very pleased to know that people are sensitive when they believe the rights of any Canadian citizen in any part of Canada have been trespassed upon.
The previous speaker made some reference to the educational qualifications of the men engaged in this security work. Like him, I have done a bit of research with respect to the report of March 31, 1960. I want to make a few comments in connection with this security work. In my opinion, in so far as security matters are concerned, the job of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police is to report the facts about an individual or a movement, not to express an opinion. Does this not in itself require a sophisticated evaluation of words and actions on the part of the person concerned. Then, how can a sophisticated evaluation be made by a person with little or no education in political theory and philosophy? This point was raised by the previous speaker when he said that, according to reports, it appears that entrance into the Royal Canadian Mounted Police requires a grade 10 education.
Now, a man can perform excellent service with a grade 10 education, but in this particular type of work I suggest that a higher educational qualification is required. A constable, I understand, could be given these tasks in connection with security work with a grade 10 education, although I understand that there are many of the investigators who have a better educational minimum than that. According to the latest Royal Canadian Mounted Police report, only three members of the force were taking full time legal training; only two were taking full time arts; only 12 were taking non-degree courses in specific subjects. According to the same report, only nine members of the force were taking languages. I am told, and I have received information in correspondence from persons connected with universities, that

many university people are under the impression that the force is somewhat unsympathetic toward intellectuals in general. I do not necessarily agree with that, but that is an opinion that has been expressed on a number of occasions. The force regards them for some reason or another with some measure of distrust. Under these circumstances, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police investigate nuclear disarmament groups which do nothing more than support proposals put forward in this house by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. In my opinion it is unlikely a communist would openly join such a movement as the ban the bomb movement or other movements of that type. These movements are supported by persons who are seriously concerned with the international situation, with the dangers of nuclear warfare. These movements, on that account, are supported by idealistic young men and women in the universities who, I think, should be given credit for being concerned with these very important questions.
Who are the persons connected with these disarmament movements and ban the bomb movements? They include Mr. Justice Thorson of the Exchequer Court of Canada; Major-General W. H. S. Macklin; Major Harry Pope, M.C., also mentioned in dispatches twice; Rabbi Feinberg; Dr. Hugh Keenleyside, chairman of the British Columbia hydro; Rev. Abbe O'Neil of Laval University; Dr. Jules Gilbert, director general of the Quebec hospital insurance service; Premier Douglas of Saskatchewan; those splendid women who are working in the Voice of Women; church leaders across Canada, a good many church groups and so on; in other words a crosssection of some of the brightest, and the most respected elements in Canadian society.
A good number of people consider that these activities carried on in this way in connection with groups of this sort, and to which I take exception, according to the reports that we have received from these people are inspired by some persons to create a fear of the social disapproval that could occur to those people who join these movements and to prevent people joining and supporting the ban the bomb movements, the Voice of Women and other organizations of that kind, through fear of loss of prestige.
In conclusion, personally and on behalf of the members of this group, on behalf of those persons who have visited me and who have written to me and on behalf of the good Canadians who are associated with these organizations, I wish to protest strongly against this type of activity by the security police, particularly when carried on in this way which shows a lack of training, a lack of discretion and a lack of understanding of

the rights and privileges that all Canadians should enjoy. It is completely out of place in a democratic country that professes great respect for the preservation of human rights and fundamental freedoms; and no one is keener on the preservation of those rights than is the Prime Minister.
I contend that we can maintain freedom only by being careful at all times and by making certain that all those who are responsible to the people of Canada practise the principles which we preach and in which we believe.

I should like to make a few brief remarks before the first item of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police is voted and especially to make a suggestion. I will not take very much of the time of the committee. I am referring here to the new regulations that have come into force in recent years with regard to pleasure boats. If I am correctly informed, pleasure boats of a certain capacity require inspection of some kind of control or supervision of their use by the R.C.M.P. In the north country or in the smaller places a difficulty arises, especially in the province of Quebec and possibly also in the province of Ontario where there are fewer R.C.M.P. officers than there are in the western provinces, for instance, where they act in both capacities, as a provincial force and as a federal force. It arises as a result of the fact that some people using pleasure boats are not following the regulations. This matter has been brought to my attention.
In a few instances in my riding some of the pleasure boat users-some of them may be young fellows or maybe we can call them water devils, young fellows who have no experience-use them in a very dangerous manner. I feel that an arrangement should be made between the R.C.M.P. and the local police, either provincial or even municipal. In certain cases this matter could be handled by the local police. The offenders assert that this matter comes under federal jurisdiction. Once they are in the middle of the river they use their boats in an objectionable manner. Some of them even take away the muffler from the motor and make more noise, sometimes within the limits of a city or a small village. They use their boats and they make the claim that once they are on the river water they come under federal jurisdiction.
I should like to make the suggestion that the R.C.M.P. make an arrangement with the local police. I understand that they cannot have officers all over the place for the purpose of checking this situation. I believe the minister has stated in speeches outside the house that we are not a police state. I appreciate this, of course. My object in making this point is not to have the R.C.M.P. prosecute everybody who uses a pleasure boat.
I should like to give an example in support of my argument. In my area of Amos we have only a few R.C.M.P. officers, and this also applies to all northern detachments, probably more particularly in Quebec and Ontario where the R.C.M.P. look after federal matters only. These R.C.M.P. officers do their very 
best in this regard in my area, but in my district they have had numerous other duties to perform, more particularly in recent times. I am sure that in such large areas they cannot be everywhere at once, but perhaps consideration could be given to having these R.C.M.P. officers work with the local municipal police force in enforcing the act. Perhaps this is already in the act but these people are not aware of it. I should like to make this suggestion to the minister.

Mr. Chairman, whilst the Minister of Justice is making notes and preparing to answer all the comments and questions of various hon. members I hope he will also consider taking a note of something about which I should like to say a few words.
I believe the Minister of Justice owes it to the House of Commons and to the people of Canada to give as concise but as full a report as he possibly can on the story and activity that broke across Canada just over a year ago, I think it was, when as a result of lengthy investigations by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in co-operation with the F.B.I. and the Hong Kong authorities we learned about the conspiracy in connection with the illegal entry into Canada of a great number of Chinese.
If my memory is correct, the Minister of Justice stated once or twice that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police had never said how many Chinese they thought were illegally in Canada. Be that as it may, somehow or other the impression got abroad-and it was really played up in the newspapers of Canada- that there were some 11,000 Chinese illegally in Canada. This, without any doubt whatsoever, cast a cloud of suspicion, and I think an unwarranted cloud of suspicion, on the entire Chinese-Canadian community. I know the Minister of Justice would be one of the first to admit that as a race Chinese-Canadians are excellent citizens. It is unfortunate that because of the publicity at the time I have mentioned the majority of these people should have come under suspicion because of the actions of the minority and because of the actions of a group of conspirators bringing into Canada, and through Canada, I understand, into the United States also, persons who were not entitled to be in this country.
As I have said, it is approximately a year ago that this information was made public and since it became such a greatly publicized story across this country. I presume that the investigation has now been carried out, but to the best of my knowledge there has never been any statement made or any information given as to the result of that investigation.
I do know, of course, from reading the newspapers that a few of these people- and I think it is a very few-have been

prosecuted. But what is the situation now? Is there any information as to how many are illegally in Canada? What is being done about them? Are they going to be allowed to stay?
I suppose that may be a question for the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. How far has the department got in this matter? Have they got anywhere, or are they going to get anywhere in finding the master minds behind this conspiracy? Has the ring been completely broken up?
I believe we should have as much information as possible on this matter. I think it is only fair that we should ask for the results, as far as they can be made public, of this now lengthy investigation by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in order that justice may be done to the vast majority of excellent Chinese-Canadians who are in this country legally, who are not involved in any way in this matter and are, as I said, good citizens.
I believe this is an important matter and I raise it because, as the Minister of Justice knows, we have a very large community of Chinese-Canadians in the city of Vancouver. In the constituency of Vancouver Centre and bordering on my own constituency I believe we have one of the largest concentrations of Chinese people in any country of the world outside China. I have in my own constituency quite a large number of Chinese-Canadians. They are excellent citizens, excellent businessmen, and they take an interest in the country and in community work. They do very well in business.
I believe that as far as possible this cloud which was cast upon these people should be dispelled. I know this cloud of suspicion was not cast upon them deliberately or purposely, but nevertheless it was cast on these people because of the situation of which the Royal Canadian Mounted Police became cognizant. That cloud should be dispelled by making public as much factual information as is possible and permissible, and making known the results of the investigation to date. We should be told the situation as it is now, and if the Minister of Justice can tell us, we should know what the situation is contemplated to be in the future. I sincerely hope that the minister, who is in charge of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, will give us the fullest possible factual report on this matter.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, several comments have been made by hon. members regarding the number of Royal Canadian Mounted Police officers who are receiving university education and training in language courses, and so on. These comments have been made, generally speaking, in the context of criticism of the methods, if not indeed of the policy, of the police in connection with security inquiries; and by the hon. member for Kootenay West, specifically in relation to the inquiry into certain activities at Laval University.
With respect to the university training program I should point out that the figures shown in this year's estimates as to the number taking that course do not relate to intelligence training as such. We have a proper proportion of persons in the security and intelligence division who have university training. Indeed, we have 20 in the headquarters research group alone who are university graduates. In addition to the provision for university training listed in the estimates, tuition fees are being paid to enable three members of the force to attend the university full-time, for six to attend university extension courses and 12 to attend the one year non-degree course and another 12 members to attend the university full-time in the faculties of law, arts, commerce and business administration. In addition we have one officer on each one of the national defence courses. These are not shown in the estimates because there is no charge made between government departments for them. It must also be borne in mind that although the minimum educational requirement on enlistment in the R.C.M.P. is grade 10 it by no means follows that we have no members joining who have higher qualifications than those of grade 10.

Sup p ly-J ustice
We have our fair proportion of university as well as high school and other graduates of standing considerably in advance of grade 10.
It may be interesting to know that the commissioner has for more than a year had a committee set up to examine this question of university training for members of the force from the point of view or whether, as is the case in some cities in the United States especially, police training courses should be university courses or whether on the other hand the desirable method is to send members of the force into the university. There are chairs in some of the United States universities, I am informed, in police training, particularly courses in criminology, scientific detection and so on. We are studying this. We have not just waited until there has been an outburst in the house. This is a matter of continuing concern, not only the question of the standard of education for recruits but the training which should be offered to members of the force after they have enlisted.
Apart from the university training and the training in the national defence college which members of the forces are receiving there is also, of course, the Canadian police college which is run by the R.C.M.P., to which our own members go and at which members of police forces across Canada and from some other countries also study. I am glad to say that we have the services there of a large number of university professors. So the training of members of the R.C.M.P. does not cease when they join the force. Not only are they trained in police methods but they are trained in research and in individual thinking on subjects not immediately connected with police work.
With respect to this difficult question of inquiries carried out by the security and intelligence branch, I am afraid I cannot at all accept as accurate all the facts contained in the newspaper report from which the hon. member read. I have not had the opportunity to study that particular report and I am not therefore able, even if I should attempt to do so at this stage, to refute it point by point. I must say I am not able to accept as accurate all which was contained therein. However, I do not mean to deny that there was some questioning of the students there. However, I have never heard it said that it was an infraction of a person's rights if he was asked a question. This is a new concept to me. I endeavoured to indicate in the brief statement I made on opening the R.C.M. Police estimates that we do have a communist threat in Canada. I am not stating anything new when I say that. It is our responsibility, then, to keep a constant check on the size, extent and efficiency of the progress being made by the communists.

It is an unfortunate fact that it is a tactic of communism to infiltrate perfectly respectable organizations. I think that most citizens, apart from an understandable irritation when they are questioned or hear of questioning, would appreciate and would be happy that the R.C.M.P., who have the responsibility in this field, are keeping a watch on these activities and endeavouring to ascertain whether and, if so, to what extent, there may have been communist infiltration into perfectly respectable organizations. Let there be no doubt about it, the respectability of the organization or the subject matter with which the organization is concerned is no guarantee against efforts to infiltrate. Thus I really do not think that any apology is necessary for the fact that inquiries have been made. Indeed, I am convinced that an apology would be necessary if we shut our eyes and said: this organization will never be the subject of communist interest so we shall not bother to inquire into it.
The R.C.M.P. is a most admirable force, but not even the R.C.M.P. can get information without asking questions. They are not mind readers. Sometimes I wish they were. I wish they were supermen so that they might know what people are thinking and would not have to ask questions at all. But since they do need to ask questions, they ask them as tactfully as they can and in a manner as convenient as possible to the person from whom they seek to get information.
