speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-33, to amend the Transport Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it gives me a great deal of pleasure to move the second reading

of Bill No. C-33, to amend the Transport Act. The proposed amendment is a simple one in its form but is of tremendous importance to the trucking industry and its 90,000 or more employees. It is designed to bring a measure of fairness and justice to the industry by providing for them the same right of appeal under the Transport Act to the Minister of Transport as other carriers have.
This is a position that has been taken by the Conservative party as a matter of principle for some time. When he was in the opposition the Prime Minister spoke very strongly in favour of the amendment that is now being proposed. In saying this I am not saying that other parties are opposed to it. I know there have been many members of all parties who have been favourable to this amendment, and this is really the first opportunity that has conveniently arisen in the house to give consideration to it. I may say that it will also be the first time that recognition of the trucking industry has been given in federal legislation, and I believe that as such it will be an acknowledgement of the great contribution made by this industry and its employees in the field of transportation in Canada and to the welfare of Canadians generally.
The rights of appeal referred to are those in connection with agreed charges of the railway. I want to emphasize in this amendment there is no intention to place the trucking industry in any special or privileged position; nor is it the intention in any way to hamper the railways. It is simply to provide the same rights of appeal under the act as all other carriers have. I would draw to the attention of the house that at the present time the act reads:
Where an agreed charge has been in effect for at least three months
(a)	any carrier or association of carriers, by water or rail, or
(b)	any association or other body representative of the shippers of any locality may complain to the minister that the agreed charge is unjustly discriminatory against a carrier-
And so forth.
The trucking industry, of course, is not covered under that right of appeal. I believe they are the ones most seriously affected under this particular provision, because an agreed charge can have the effect, and often does, of eliminating whole segments of the trucking industry from the competitive field of transportation. I believe it only fair and reasonable that they should have the right to appeal when such a case arises.
Agreed charges do not have to be compensatory to the railroad. Section 32 of the Transport Act says:
Notwithstanding anything in the Railway Act or in this act, a carrier may make such charges for
Transport Act
the transport from one point in Canada to another point in Canada of goods of a shipper as are agreed between the carrier and the shipper.
In other words, it is whatever agreement is arrived at between the carrier and the shipper, and that becomes the rate that is then in force. As I say, that can and does often have the effect of eliminating segments of the trucking industry. Many of the agreed charges specify that 100 per cent of the commodities shipped must go by rail; that truck transport cannot be used at all. Others specify that 95 per cent must go by rail, and so on. I am sure the house will agree that this is a very extraordinary method of rate making and agreement and is one that can have a serious effect on the trucking industry and, by the same token, have a serious effect on the competitive aspects of our transportation system.
This amendment then proposes that any association or other body representative of the motor vehicle operators in Canada or of a province thereof be given the same rights under the act to apply to the minister that other carriers have.
To follow this through I would draw to the attention of the house subsection 4 of section 33 of the Transport Act, which in its language, in my opinion makes it very plain that the trucking industry should be included in this right of appeal because of the very wording of the section. I think it will show quite clearly that it was meant and should have been meant to apply to the trucking industry. The subsection reads:
If the board, after a hearing, finds that the agreed charge is undesirable in the public interest on the ground that it is unjustly discriminatory against any person complaining against it or places his business or any other form of transportation services at an unfair disadvantage or on any other ground, the board may make an order varying or cancelling the agreed charge or such other order as in the circumstances it considers proper.
Now, I think by the words in this clause stating that where it believes any other form of transportation service is at an unfair disadvantage it was intended that it should have the right to appeal under this act.
I am sure the house will want to give speedy consideration to this measure. I do not think I need to go any further into the history of the act. I have spoken on it on many occasions in the house and I have spoken to many hon. members individually. I know there is wide support for the measure and it is my hope that we shall be able to proceed with it through the committee stage today.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR APPLICATION BY TRUCKERS TO MINISTER ON AGREED CHARGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy once again to find myself in agreement with the hon. member for

Transport Act
Vaneouver-Kingsway. In a matter under discussion in this house, whether it be legislation, estimates or resolutions, it is so easy to find oneself in disagreement with members on the other side of the house. Therefore, I think it is comforting from time to time to see that members do agree either individually or when speaking on behalf of their parties to a bill which comes up in this manner.
In so far as this bill to amend the Transport Act is concerned there is not the slightest difficulty on this side of the house. We will support the bill. Lest anyone from the other side rises to say that when this matter was under discussion under a previous administration a different attitude was taken from that taken by myself at this time perhaps I should give a short explanation.
In the first place I think I should say, and agree with the hon. member who has just spoken, that it is a fact beyond doubt that the trucking industry has made a tremendous contribution to our transportation systems in Canada. That was proven when there was a railway strike some years ago. The trucking industry showed then without any doubt what it was able to accomplish, together with the air industry, in transporting goods from one end of the country to the other. Therefore, on that general statement there can be little or no difference of opinion. The trucking industry is of tremendous importance to the economy of Canada. It has contributed a great deal in the field of transportation.
If one looks at the bill it strikes one at first blush that perhaps there is no necessity for including the amendment which my hon. friend has put forward. But if there is any doubt in the mind of the house or particularly in the mind of the trucking industry, then I see no reason why this amendment should not be included in the act. The section reads:
Where an agreed charge has been in effect for at least three months.
(a)	any carrier, or association of carriers by water or rail,
(b)	any association or other body representative of the shippers of any locality,
may complain to the minister-
It would seem to one at first blush that perhaps this in itself is sufficient to meet the requirements of the hon. member. He thinks it is not and I take it that the trucking industry thinks it is not. If that is the case, I see no reason why the language should not be clarified by adding paragraph (c) which would read as follows:
(c)	any association or other body representative of the motor vehicle operators of Canada or of a province thereof-

They could then complain to the minister in the circumstances set out in the balance of the section.
I come now to a discussion of the matter which took place when I was not a member of the house, not that that makes any difference. At that time my successor, the hon. Mr. Marler, had for consideration in the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines certain amendments to section 33. At that time a motion was moved by Mr. Lang-lois and seconded by Mr. Cavers that section 33 be deleted and replaced by a new section including subsection 1 as it now reads in Bill No. C-33 with, of course, certain other additions. Perhaps I might put that subsection on the record. It reads as follows:
33 (1) Where an agreed charge has been in effect for a least three months.
(a)	any carrier or association of carriers, by water or rail, or
(b)	any association or other body representative of the shippers of any locality
may complain to the minister that the agreed charge is unjustly discriminatory against a carrier or a shipper or places his business at an unfair disadvantage, and the minister may, if he is satisfied that in the public interest the complaint should be investigated, refer the complaint to the board for investigation.
I will not read the rest of the amendment which was proposed by Mr. Langlois and seconded by Mr. Cavers. At a later time in the hearings the present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) moved an amendment to section 33 to this effect, that after the words "association of carriers by water or rail" the words "or any association of motor vehicle transport operators" be added. That amendment was defeated. Now the hon. member for Vaneouver-Kingsway (Mr. Browne) brings in another amendment which I think goes further than that of the Secretary of State for External Affairs because it covers a broader field and is, I think, more explanatory.
I do not think I need to explain away the attitude taken by the committee at that time other than to say this. There was a long discussion of the bill, and while this amendment was of importance perhaps the committee did not realize at the time just what the meaning was or again it may well be that the committee thought that the words found in paragraph (b), "any association or other body representative of the shippers of any locality" were sufficiently broad and wide to cover the motor vehicle operators of Canada. Whether or not that is the case I do not know because I was not there. In any event, I have no hesitation in saying that while it may be that the language is sufficient to cover the industry, if the industry feels and if the house feels that it is not sufficiently broad I

cannot see any reason why the broader language should not be accepted. Having said that, I do not think I need add anything further except to say that we on this side of the house will support the bill as proposed by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak briefly on only one point with relation to the bill. The hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) raised a point as to the necessity of the wording in the amendment. I support the amendment because I think this wording is an absolute necessity. The matter has been before the board on occasion and the board has ruled that these carriers do not come under the act. For that reason I think it is absolutely necessary that this wording should be included. Certainly there must be an appeal because the trucking business has grown throughout Canada to such an extent that when an agreed rate is fixed that industry should have the right to make representations where the rate would tend to discriminate against the industry as a whole.
As mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Browne), it could be that an agreed charge would require total carriage by rail to the exclusion of trucks everywhere, and to my mind this is wrong and discriminatory. On these two grounds I would recommend that the amendment be passed.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR APPLICATION BY TRUCKERS TO MINISTER ON AGREED CHARGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find myself in almost the same position as the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier). When we in this group first read the amendment and checked it against the original section we were definitely of the opinion that the present wording was sufficient to meet what the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Browne) has in mind. I think it is easily understood why that was our opinion. As hon. members know, the wording in the existing section is that any association or other body representative of the shippers of any locality may complain. Logically we took that to mean that the trucking industry was a shipper. What else can the trucking industry be if it is not a shipper just the same as the railways and water carriers are? We do not see why that is not the correct interpretation but if it is felt that it is necessary to make it absolutely clear that the trucking industry is a shipper and is entitled to the same right to complain if it feels that it is being unjustly discriminated against, then most certainly we have no objection to what is sought to be done through the medium of the bill.
It must be recognized, of course, that this amendment will in no way whatsoever solve
Transport Act
the problems or resolve the complexities of the transportation industry in Canada which is made up of the truckers, the water carriers, the railroads and the air carriers. It is almost inevitable that there will be competition between them. If I may say so, it does seem a little amusing and paradoxical that those who so heartily and enthusiastically endorse competition do not like it when it happens to affect a particular individual or company or industry in which they are interested. Whether it is just or unjust, it is still competition. However, irrespective of that, we have the rather amazing and paradoxical situation that when the competition gets tough they want to eliminate the competition. I say that as long as we do have this system it does seem obvious that discriminatory action should not be permitted in order to maintain this transportation industry.
As has already been pointed out, the trucking industry is an important and integral part of the transportation industry of our country. I should like to add to the words of the hon. member for Laurier by saying that the people of this country would have been in a most difficult position on more than one occasion if it had not been for the trucking industry. I refer not only to a situation which occurs during a rail strike but also to situations which arise as the result of the abandonment of lines by the railways or a curtailment of service. This has happened in British Columbia on the Kettle valley line. We would be in a difficult position there if it were not for the trucking industry. There is a daily movement by means of refrigerated trucks of the vegetables, hard and soft fruits for which the consumers are waiting.
We say, therefore, that basically we see no objection to this amendment. I have already said that, irrespective of the economics of the situation, if there is one phase of the transportation industry which is subjected to unjust discrimination based on the completely unfair competition of a rate which may have been set at an unprofitable level, then surely that segment of the industry has a right to object. As I say, Mr. Speaker, in view of these circumstances this amending bill which has been moved by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway will most certainly receive the endorsation and support of this group.

Mr. Speaker, the present bill is similar to bills introduced in previous sessions by the hon. member. On previous occasions the attitude of the government has been that we should wait for the report of the royal commission on transportation before we acquiesced to the passage of the bill or before taking a definite attitude toward the bill. At

Transport Act
the moment we have received the first part of the MacPherson commission report, and I am expressing the opinion of the government at the moment when I say that this bill will not interfere with any of the recommendations that commission has brought forward so far. I am very pleased to say, in the name of the government, that we intend to ask every member in this house to support this bill.
I know, Mr. Speaker, that it is a bit unusual, but I should like to say, first of all, that this bill is a recognition of the great services the trucking industry has rendered to the Canadian people on a day to day basis. This bill, to some people, might not represent a tremendous change. On the other hand, as the hon. member said earlier, it represents the first time that the trucking industry has been recognized in a federal statute. I want to congratulate the hon. member upon his presentation of the bill and for the keen interest he has always taken in transportation questions, both here in the house and in the various committees.
The other day the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) paid tribute to the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway for the deep knowledge he exhibited of the very complicated question of freight rates. There is no doubt that freight rates have become exceedingly complicated with the passage of time, and anyone who discusses these matters with a profound knowledge must have worked tremendously hard to digest all this information. I want to congratulate the hon. member upon the very clear explanation he made in presenting his bill and the recognition he has brought to the trucking industry of Canada.
Yesterday, I had the privilege of meeting, with the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and two of my colleagues, a group representing the trucking association of Canada. We discussed, for about an hour and a half, the various problems of the trucking industry and I must say it was an extremely interesting meeting. We might not, at all times, have seen eye to eye on the various problems they were bringing before us, but I can assure the house that the representations they made to us will receive most serious consideration. I appeal to the whole house to support this bill. I should like to say also, in the name of the government, that if the mover of this bill desires, and the house is willing, the government will consent to all three stages of the bill being passed today.

Therefore, because the trucking industry has grown in prominence and its needs are not being met according to the interests of the trucking industry itself and because they will be better served through this amendment, I am in agreement with the course the minister has suggested and would be willing to give the bill three readings today.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF JURISDICTION TO INCLUDE DIVORCE

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: EXTENSION OF JURISDICTION TO INCLUDE DIVORCE
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-35, respecting the jurisdiction of the Exchequer Court of Canada.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I had not thought that this bill would be discussed today. We were rather hopeful that, before it was reached, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) would have given some indication that this was an acceptable procedure to which the government was giving some consideration. In introducing this bill may I say that it is one that has been suggested by other people before I came to parliament and that since my arrival it has been presented by me several times. It is a bill which would, in a manner, solve the problem confronting the House of Commons, the Senate and the people of the provinces of Quebec and Newfoundland. It would provide a court procedure by means of which to handle divorce actions from both the province of Newfoundland and the province of Quebec.
In connection with the use of the petition method where the petitioner petitions the federal government for a divorce one of the problems we face at the present time is this. Although there is not any question that the parliament of Canada is the highest federal court, we as a federal court have not the machinery, the rules or the regulations by means of which to handle in a satisfactory manner actions of this type. At the present time the Senate is serving this function and a review takes place in the House of Commons. Over the years this method has been proved to be a highly unsatisfactory one. The reason for suggesting the exchequer court that has a correlation between the lower fact that the exchequer court is a federal court. It has an advantage that we are not suggesting in this bill be used. However, it has an advantage that the exchequer court can move from place to place and therefore it could at any time be closer to the petitioners-at that time I suppose they would be the plaintiffs-than is the adjudicating body under the present system. It also is a court that has correlation between the lower superior courts and the Supreme Court of Canada, something that makes it possible that the one court can inquire into those abuses that sometimes take place. At the present time we find that one of the abuses is perjury. This is indicated by some of the evidence and declarations that are made before the

Exchequer Court
members of the committee. There are also false statements made in some of the divorce petitions. These matters are brought to
the attention of the house and the Minister of Justice by members of the committee.
This has been found to be unsatisfactory because the Minister of Justice does not act in the position of proctor for the Senate and the House of Commons. The minister has to operate within his own limited jurisdiction as the Attorney General of Canada, and for this reason this method has been found to be highly unsatisfactory.
The exchequer court has the advantage that its jurisdiction can be extended. Judges of the exchequer court could be empowered to handle cases sent to them from this parliament. It is not necessary to have a higher court than the exchequer court. It is well recognized that at the present time the exchequer court handles financial problems in the main. It handles appeals in financial cases. Its jurisdiction in the main is in the field of finance, but we believe that two or three judges could be attached to the exchequer court and a clause put in the appropriate act which would empower exchequer court judges, for a particular, specified length of time, to meet only in the city of Ottawa and hear divorce actions.
They should not have the right to hear divorce actions in the provinces of Quebec or Newfoundland. The ultimate aim, of course, is for the provincial governments to assume jurisdiction over divorce. However, we know there are reasons why the province of Quebec does not want to set up divorce courts. Other provinces have other reasons, The province of Ontario set up divorce courts by petitioning the federal government for the right to do so not too long ago.
The province of Quebec does not want divorce courts, and we can understand why that is so. Within our federal jurisdiction we have the divorce act of 1930 governing divorce procedures. This act was given to Canada through the British North America Act and is included as one of the commitments in that act for which the federal government has responsibility. Therefore if these provinces do not wish to assume the responsibility of having their own divorce courts, we have the obligation to do something about it. It seems to me there could be little objection to a federal court being established for this purpose. The matter of divorce thus could be handled in a much more satisfactory manner. Divorce actions should be included in the jurisdiction of the exchequer court. Hon. members will be familiar with the statements 
made by the Minister of Justice only recently. The minister said he would consider having the exchequer court assume this responsibility.
It should be borne in mind that this would not solve all the problems that have been raised over the past year or two. If the exchequer court were given jurisdiction over divorce this would not mean that court would have the right to award custody of children, which is at the present and will remain the sole responsibility of the provincial government. The exchequer court would not have the right to decide the question of alimony or maintenance for the children. If this jurisdiction were given to the exchequer court it would not carry with it the right to interfere with the licensing of agencies that are concerned at the present time and will continue to be concerned with divorce procedures. These changes cannot and will not be eliminated by any intervention on the part of the federal government in the field of changing the jurisdiction of divorce for the provinces of Newfoundland and Quebec.
Another problem that will remain is a matter which affects provincial governments entirely. I refer to the matter of the licensing of bailiffs and other officials who are involved in divorce actions. The Senate has made changes in its procedure. It has a set of rules under which it operates. These rules are similar to those under which the courts operate. The Senate has set up the grounds for divorce in the provinces of Quebec and Newfoundland and it has now stipulated that there must be an affidavit of sorts signed by the party concerned and returned to the Senate indicating that the respondent and the corespondent have been notified of the action against them, and have been notified of their right to a hearing in the action.
However, this procedure just does not work and it will not work even if the act is changed so that jurisdiction is given to the exchequer court. I say this will not work because in the province of Quebec we find that many of these petitions contain false statements. Petitions contain evidence that a bailiff has gone to a particular house, a particular party has made a statement and the bailiff has received from him a signature to a statement saying that he is the party involved; it is his name that is being used either as that of the respondent or corespondent. Yet when we write letters to these people and later have a tracer put on them we find that in many cases there is no such address. In fact, in 30 cases out of 240 divorce actions we found there were no such addresses in the city of Montreal. We found that the addresses physically

just did not exist. Yet we have a bailiff swearing a document to the effect that the address does exist, and producing a signature which he testifies is the signature of the person whose name appears as that of either the corespondent or respondent. When tracers are carried out by the post office, they confirm that these addresses do not exist and, as I have said, we have had 30 such instances where the address has been false.
This is another of the malpractices that flows from the problem of split jurisdiction under which we operate and under which it appears we may operate for sometime to come. There are advantages in establishing this jurisdiction in the exchequer court. This method would have more advantages than any we have investigated to date.
As I have said, the ideal and the final solution to the problem would be for these provinces to come to parliament and ask by petition to be given the right to set up their own divorce courts and handle divorce actions in their own way. In this way they would be able to assume the responsibility for the custody of the children, for the maintenance of those children, for alimony payments and for the legal operation of the court.
The exchequer court has some of the powers necessary for the judicial operation of a divorce court. There are officers attached to the exchequer court who are in a position to take affidavits and make investigations. It is not unreasonable to expect that if this action is taken by the house-perhaps not today but some time in the near future-the exchequer court would have the power to ask for and to use the services of the Queen's proctor. The Queen's proctor would be able to do the job which the hon. member for Skeena and myself have been trying to do in our own very limited way. I refer to investigating the offences that are taking place under the procedure which is now in effect. The hon. member and myself have done this in all the cases that have passed through the Senate to date.
We have written to every corespondent and every respondent. Hon. members of the house would be very interested in seeing some of the replies we have received. Our reason for writing to these people is only to see whether they knew they had been named in the particular case; whether they knew they were being divorced, on the one hand, or knew, on the other hand, that they were involved in the divorce and adultery charges that had been made.

speechtext:
Would the hon. member permit a question? We have listened to this debate over many hours, over many years. Exactly what does he want?
Exchequer Court

subtopic: EXTENSION OF JURISDICTION TO INCLUDE DIVORCE
speechtext: What is your question?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: EXTENSION OF JURISDICTION TO INCLUDE DIVORCE
speechtext:
I do not know what the question is. I could probably answer it by saying that if we had not been in such a hurry with the previous bill we should not be discussing this at all this afternoon. We are offering a solution to this particular problem of divorce which has plagued Canada since the passing of the British North America Act. I am sure that if Sir John A. Macdonald had known the problems which were going to arise he would not have placed upon the federal government the responsibility for divorce as it exists at present. He would have given it to the provinces in the first place. However, this responsibility does now rest upon the dominion government under the terms of that act and we are suggesting that the least objectionable way of discharging it would be to delegate it to the exchequer court. I have sat in on the procedures being used at the present time and I am sure many of the legal people involved have cause to wonder at the system which we adopt. Some hon. gentlemen, with the best of intentions, will get up and ask questions which bear no relation to the establishment of the adultery charge which should be the only ground for the divorce as at present constituted. I am sure many of the lawyers would be happy to see the whole question brought within the jurisdiction of a court which would function and operate in the manner of a court.
If we brought these cases into the exchequer court we would enable those who seek fundamental justice to have the right of appeal. Appeals could be taken to the supreme court and at least one of the difficulties now being experienced would be eliminated. We in parliament have no right to marry people. If we were to act as an appeal court-if we looked back over one of these cases and found that the evidence was a lie and that we had been completely deceived, and then decided that the petition should be rescinded instead of granted-we should in effect, be remarrying people who had been divorced, and that would be an impossibility.
It is almost six o'clock. I think there should be more time to discuss this important matter but we are not too concerned, because the minister has said he is giving consideration to it. I really believe that the Minister of Justice should bring in this bill rather than myself. The measure does not establish a divorce court which would operate in the province of Quebec. It does no more than make available to the citizens of Quebec a proper court procedure which is not available to them at the present time.

Business of the House

subtopic: EXTENSION OF JURISDICTION TO INCLUDE DIVORCE
speechtext:
I wish the hon. member had proceeded with his argument. It was most interesting, and in another three or four minutes he might have succeeded in convincing members of the house that they should support this bill. In the limited time I have available may I say that I have every sympathy with the objectives he has in mind in commending this bill. I have sat on the committee which deals with these divorce cases. I think there are other things we could more usefully be employed in doing, and I do not like the methods used in it. However, may I put one or two suggestions to the hon. member, and when the bill again comes forward for discussion he may be able to make use of some of them.
The exchequer court is composed of judges who deal with a specialized type of work- patent, copyright and similar matters arising out of legislation in this field-cases where the crown is involved. They have built up specialized skill and knowledge and I should hardly think that the learned judges of the exchequer court would be the proper people to whom we should allocate responsibility for settling these divorce cases. May I also point out that there is no provision for appeal in respect of divorce cases from decisions of the exchequer court as now constituted. People who resorted to it and wished to appeal would have no machinery available to them.
Third, may I say I do not like the limited ground for divorce which the hon. member has set out in this bill, a ground confined to adultery, having in mind the wider grounds which are now generally accepted and which form the basis of the United Kingdom law.
May I call it six o'clock?
